```{r}
design$present <- design$s >= .entry[design$p]
design$Property <- factor(.props[design$p], levels = rev(.props))
design$Session  <- factor(paste0("S", design$s), levels = paste0("S", .sess))
# The session axis is deliberately ORDINAL, not metric: it encodes which property was
# tested when, and makes no claim about elapsed time. Because the intervals are in fact
# very unequal (one week between Sessions 2-4, about four months before Session 6), the
# spacing is annotated numerically rather than drawn to scale -- drawing it to scale
# would also invite a false reading, since attrition over the retention interval is
# heavy (see @fig-flow).
ggplot(design, aes(x = Session, y = Property)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = present, fill = present), size = 5, colour = "grey25", stroke = 0.4) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 21, `TRUE` = 21), guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "white", `TRUE` = "grey25"), name = NULL,
                    labels = c(`FALSE` = "Not yet introduced", `TRUE` = "Present and tested")) +
  annotate("segment", x = c(1, 2), xend = c(2, 3), y = 0.42, yend = 0.42,
           colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.3,
           arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.07, "cm"), ends = "both")) +
  annotate("text", x = c(1.5, 2.5), y = 0.60, label = "1 week", size = 2.8, colour = "grey45") +
  annotate("segment", x = 3, xend = 4, y = 0.42, yend = 0.42, colour = "grey25",
           arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.10, "cm"), ends = "both")) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.5, y = 0.60, size = 2.8, colour = "grey25",
           label = "~4 months (retention)") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.4, 3.5), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "Session", y = NULL) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = 21, size = 3))) +
  les_theme(10) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top",
        plot.margin = margin(4, 10, 12, 6))
```

Three quantities operationalise our hypotheses. The grammaticality effect
(the amplitude or accuracy difference between ungrammatical and grammatical trials)
indexes whether a property is processed grammatically at all. The
grammaticality $\times$ session interaction indexes *learning*: the sharpening of
that effect with exposure. Its modulation by language, the grammaticality $\times$
session $\times$ language term, indexes *source-language transfer*, whether learning is
faster or stronger for the language whose prior structures align with the target
property. A derived Session 4 $\to$ Session 6 contrast then indexes how the
grammaticality effect changes across the consolidation interval. The language advantage
evaluated at a property's first session, derived from the same draws, indexes whether
that advantage was in place when the property was first probed.

The transfer accounts make no prediction about the retention interval, since they
concern the initial state and the course of acquisition. The expectation for that
interval comes from the training literature cited above, in which a grammaticality
response that has emerged during training holds or grows across months without exposure
[@morganshort2012plos]. If transfer is property-specific, that profile may differ
between the property with a first-language analogue and the two without. The retention
contrasts therefore characterise the trajectory. They do not test between the accounts.

The two families of account are separated here by which prior grammar each engages and
by when its influence should appear. Gender agreement is the only property with a
first-language analogue, and so the only one on which the two miniature languages stand
in different relations to a prior grammar. Differential object marking and verb--object
number agreement are novel to Norwegian and English alike and are realised identically in
the two miniature languages. Property-level congruence therefore predicts no group
difference on them under either family, and they serve as controls. A wholesale account,
on which one prior grammar supplies the initial state for the L3 grammar as a whole, must
also say which
grammar is selected. The Typological Primacy Model selects the source from a rapid
typological assessment led by lexical similarity, and the design speaks to that cue
directly. Each miniature language draws its content words from one of the prior
languages, so lexically led selection points each group to the language its miniature
language is built on, English for Mini-English and Norwegian for Mini-Norwegian. On that
selection, a wholesale account predicts a Mini-Norwegian advantage on gender agreement,
present from that property's first session, because the projected Norwegian grammar
supplies both the gender system and its suffixal format. It predicts no group
difference on the control properties, which neither projected grammar encodes. A
property-by-property account predicts the same confinement of the advantage to gender
agreement but a different onset, with the advantage emerging only as the learner detects
the structural match. Under the source selection
this design supports, then, the two families agree on where the gender-agreement
advantage should appear and differ only on when. The diagnostic quantity is therefore
the advantage at the property's first session, which wholesale projection predicts to
be present and a property-by-property account predicts to be absent or small. Growth of
the advantage across sessions is predicted by the property-by-property account and
permitted by wholesale projection, which constrains the initial state and says nothing
about subsequent learning [@gonzalezalonso2017], so growth alone favours the former
without excluding the latter.

The L2 Status Factor makes a further prediction of its own. If the second language is the
default source, both groups project English, which encodes none of the three properties,
so property-level congruence predicts no group difference anywhere. If projecting a
source whose morphological format matches the input eases processing of that input at
all, the beneficiary under an English default is the Mini-English group, whose miniature
language is built on English-like free morphology. In no derivation does an L2 default predict a
Mini-Norwegian advantage. This design discriminates the two families less sharply than a
design contrasting two candidate source grammars would, and we return to the point in the
Limitations.

Alongside the region-averaged models, we ask whether grammaticality is decodable from the
whole-scalp voltage pattern at each moment. A multivariate decoder can detect a
distributed violation response too weak to move any single region's mean. Its
cross-language generalisation asks whether the pattern that separates the conditions in
one mini-language also separates them in the other. Its cross-property generalisation
tests a further prediction. If the grammaticality response were largely a domain-general
salience or integration signal [@sassenhagen2019; @aurnhammer2023], a decoder trained on
one property should transfer to the others. If each property recruits its own code, as
the fractionation of the late positivity [@kaan2003] and the separable developmental
courses of agreement features [@alemanbanon2018] suggest, it should not. No null
distribution was computed for either generalisation analysis, so both are reported as
descriptive probes.

# Method

## Participants

In total, `r flow_n("enrolled")` Norwegian--English bilinguals (first
language Norwegian, second language English) took part, each assigned to learn one
of the two miniature languages. Assignment followed a fixed rule on the participant
identifier, giving `r flow_n("enrolled", "n_mini_english")` Mini-English and
`r flow_n("enrolled", "n_mini_norwegian")` Mini-Norwegian learners, so language is a
between-participants factor. Of the `r pstat("n_lhq3", "value", 0)` participants
with a Language History Questionnaire record [LHQ3: @lhq3], the mean age was
`r pstat("age_years")` years ($SD = `r pstat("age_years", "sd")`$, range
`r pstat("age_years", "vmin", 0)`--`r pstat("age_years", "vmax", 0)`).`r minors_note()`
Of the same record, `r pstat("sex_female", "value", 0)` identified as female,
`r pstat("sex_male", "value", 0)` as male and `r pstat("sex_nonbinary", "value", 0)`
as non-binary (`r pstat("sex_undisclosed", "value", 0)` did not disclose). Among the
`r pstat("hand_reported_n", "value", 0)` who reported handedness,
`r pstat("hand_right", "value", 0)` were right-handed and
`r pstat("hand_left", "value", 0)` left-handed. English had been
acquired early (age of first exposure $M = `r pstat("eng_aoa_listen")`$ years,
$SD = `r pstat("eng_aoa_listen", "sd")`$) and used for many years
($M = `r pstat("eng_years")`$, $SD = `r pstat("eng_years", "sd")`$), with high
self-rated proficiency ($M = `r pstat("eng_l2_proficiency", "value", 2)`$ of 1,
$SD = `r pstat("eng_l2_proficiency", "sd", 2)`$). `r other_lang_sentence()`

Attrition increased across the training: of the `r flow_n("enrolled")` who began,
`r flow_n("attended_S3")` remained at Session 3, `r flow_n("attended_S4")` at
Session 4, and `r flow_n("attended_S6")` completed the Session 6 retention test.
The ERP analyses draw on the `r flow_n("usable_erp")` participants with usable
single-trial EEG (`r flow_n("usable_erp", "n_mini_english")` Mini-English,
`r flow_n("usable_erp", "n_mini_norwegian")` Mini-Norwegian). The fitted ERP models
also require the L1-dominance covariate described under *Data analysis*, and the trials
of a participant without that score are dropped by listwise deletion, so the
gender-agreement models were fitted to `r erp_model_n("gender_agreement")`
participants, the differential-object-marking models to
`r erp_model_n("differential_object_marking")` and the verb--object number-agreement
models to `r erp_model_n("verb_object_number_agreement")`. The
grammaticality-judgement analyses draw on `r flow_n("usable_accuracy")` participants
(@fig-flow). The project was registered with the Norwegian Agency for Shared Services in
Education and Research (Sikt; project 2559611). All procedures complied
with the relevant laws and institutional guidelines, the privacy rights of the participants
were observed, and every participant gave written informed consent.

```{r}
#| label: fig-flow
#| fig-cap: "Participant Flow"
#| apa-note: "Each stage spans the full enrolled cohort: the solid block is the participants still present, split by mini-language, and the faint block completing the bar is those no longer present, so cumulative attrition is visible as the unfilled area. Tapering bands connect consecutive stages, and each transition is annotated with the number lost and the percentage retained. The upper tier tracks enrolment and attendance at the four sessions this paper analyses. Sessions 1 and 5 are online cognitive sessions belonging to the companion paper and are omitted. The lower tier holds the analysis samples, which draw on the whole cohort pooled across sessions and not on Session 6, so bands are drawn only within a tier, where the subset relation holds. Two features of the cohort prevent a strictly nested reading: one participant missed Session 5 and returned for Session 6, and one contributes usable grammaticality judgements but no usable ERP."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
if (!is.null(flow_tbl)) {
  fl <- flow_tbl[order(flow_tbl$order), ]
  fl <- fl[!is.na(fl$n_total), ]
  fl <- fl[!grepl("\\(Paper 2\\)", fl$label), ]          # this paper's flow only
  fl$label <- sub("\\s*\\(Paper 1\\)", "", fl$label)      # the tag is now redundant
  # Sessions 1 and 5 are online cognitive sessions that contribute nothing to this
  # paper's measures; showing them here would imply attrition this paper suffered.
  fl <- fl[!fl$stage %in% c("attended_S1", "attended_S5"), ]
  d <- data.frame(
    label = fl$label, n = fl$n_total,
    n_a = fl$n_mini_english, n_b = fl$n_mini_norwegian,
    tier = ifelse(grepl("^(enrolled|attended)", fl$stage),
                  "Enrolment and attendance", "Analysis samples"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  # Flag the one participant whose judgement data outlives their ERP data, so the
  # gap between the two analysis bars is explained rather than left as an oddity.
  d$note <- ifelse(d$label == "Usable single-trial ERP data",
                   "one participant has usable\njudgement data but not ERP", NA_character_)
  les_funnel(d, base_size = LES_FIG_BASE_SIZE)
} else {
  cat("*Participant-flow diagram will appear once `_sample_flow.csv` is present.*")
}
```

## Design and materials

The longitudinal artificial-language paradigm implemented here is that of the wider
project reported by @gonzalezalonso2025. Within each language, the design crosses
grammaticality (contrast coded
grammatical $= +0.5$, ungrammatical $= -0.5$) with session (the cumulative exposure
schedule above) within participants, and language between participants
(Mini-Norwegian $= +0.5$, Mini-English $= -0.5$), so a positive language-bearing
coefficient indicates a larger value for the Mini-Norwegian group. The three
properties were analysed separately. Each was probed with 48 grammatical and 48
ungrammatical sentences per session, built from a closed lexicon of twelve nouns, twelve
adjectives, twelve transitive verbs and twelve proper names per language. A third,
ancillary violation type was recorded but is not analysed here. Each sentence frame was
presented in both a grammatical and an ungrammatical version. The two miniature
languages draw on separate content lexicons, Mini-English building its nouns,
adjectives, verbs and names on English stems and Mini-Norwegian on
Norwegian stems. The critical word
carried the EEG trigger that defined the single-trial time-lock.

The two miniature languages share the same invented grammatical morphemes (the
determiners *je*/*ze*/*jer*/*zer*, the object marker *fi*, the verbal suffix *-evo*
and the adjectival agreement suffixes). They differ in one structural dimension,
determiner position, and that difference is the pivot of the transfer contrast.
Subject--verb gender agreement is built on a two-way common/neuter distinction, as
in real Norwegian. In Mini-English, the determiner is a free prenominal word that
marks gender and number (*je*/*ze* for common/neuter singular, *jer*/*zer* for
the plural), as English articles are free-standing. In Mini-Norwegian, the same
gender--number determiner is a bound suffix on the noun (e.g. *gateje*/*gatejer*),
as the Norwegian definite article is suffixal. In both languages, the predicate
adjective carries a matching agreement suffix, on which the gender-agreement
violation is realised. Differential object marking is a free particle *fi* placed
before the object noun phrase, identical in the two languages, with the violation
omitting it. Verb--object number agreement is a verbal suffix *-evo* that marks the
verb to agree with a plural object, again identical across languages, with the
violation a number mismatch between verb and object.

These three properties map onto the learners' existing grammars differently, which
is what the language factor exploits. Grammatical gender expressed through a
suffixed determiner is a property of the learners' first language, Norwegian, but
not of their second language, English. The Mini-Norwegian realisation therefore
aligns closely with the first-language grammar, whereas the Mini-English realisation expresses
a feature that English does not encode (gender) through an English-like free
determiner. Differential object marking and verb--object number agreement, by
contrast, are absent from both Norwegian and English, so neither is supported by a
prior grammar in either group.

## Procedure

Sentences were presented one word at a time in the centre of the screen (rapid serial
visual presentation, RSVP) using OpenSesame 3.3.14. Word duration was a deterministic
function of word length. A non-critical word was shown for
$250 + 35 \times (\text{characters} - 3)$ ms, floored at 250 ms, giving durations of
250--600 ms. The critical word was shown for 40 ms less than a non-critical word of the
same length (210--560 ms). Non-critical words followed one another at a stimulus-onset
asynchrony of approximately 505 ms. At the critical word, the script held the asynchrony
fixed at approximately 750 ms, lengthening the following blank interval to compensate for
the varying word duration. The timing of the post-critical region therefore did not depend
on the length of the critical word. The critical word occupied the third or fourth position and
was followed by three to six further words. Presentation was entirely
experimenter-paced. Nothing in the sentence stream depended on the participant, so a
condition difference in reading speed cannot shift the epoch. The grammaticality judgement
was requested only after the final word of the sentence, never during it, and was made with
a two-button response (left = grammatical, right = violation). No motor response therefore
fell inside the analysed epoch.

This timing has one consequence for the late window. The raw presentation logs record
all `r rsvp_tim("n_trials", big = TRUE)` critical-word trials, a census taken before any
EEG-side exclusion, so its count exceeds the modelled trial numbers. In that census,
exactly one subsequent word onset falls within 900 ms
of the critical word (the per-trial maximum is
`r rsvp_tim("max_onsets_within_900ms")`), at `r rsvp_tim("next_onset_min_ms")`--`r rsvp_tim("next_onset_max_ms")` ms
(median `r rsvp_tim("next_onset_median_ms")` ms). The final roughly 150 ms of the
400--900 ms measurement window therefore contains the beginning of the response to the
following word. This is unavoidable in connected-sentence RSVP at this rate, and it is
constant across conditions because the post-critical asynchrony is held fixed, so it cannot
manufacture a grammaticality effect. Late-window amplitudes should nonetheless be read as
containing that overlap. They are not a pure response to the critical word.

## EEG acquisition and single-trial ERP quantification

Continuous EEG was recorded with a 32-channel Brain Products LiveAmp system, using active
electrodes in an extended 10--20 layout with the CACS-32 cap montage recorded in the data
headers. The sampling rate was 500 Hz and the online passband DC--131 Hz, with no online
notch filter. The 131 Hz anti-aliasing low-pass is a causal acquisition filter, so it
imposes no phase distortion of the kind that motivates the offline filter choices set out
below.

Three channel counts appear in what follows, and they refer to different things, so we
set them out once. Thirty-two electrodes were recorded. Two of them, TP9 and TP10, become
the offline linked-mastoid reference and are therefore not analysed as signals. FCz served
as the online reference and is recovered as a channel when the data are re-referenced. The
remaining 30 electrodes are the ones assigned to the nine analysis regions, so they are
what the region-averaged amplitude models use and what the scalp maps interpolate across.
The decoder ignores the region map and takes every EEG channel available in
all contributing sessions, which is those 30 plus the recovered FCz, giving 31 features.
The LiveAmp's three accelerometer traces (`x_dir`, `y_dir`, `z_dir`) are movement signals,
not brain signals, and are excluded throughout. The Session 2 exports additionally retain
TP9, TP10 and the accelerometer channels, whereas the Session 3, 4 and 6 exports do not,
which is why the decoder uses only the channels common to every session. Offline, in
BrainVision Analyzer, the data were re-referenced to
the mastoids and then band-pass filtered with zero-phase-shift (forward and reverse)
Butterworth IIR filters, high-pass 0.1 Hz and low-pass 30 Hz, each specified in Analyzer as
fourth order (24 dB per octave). Because the filters are applied in both directions, the
effective roll-off is approximately double that figure. No notch filter was applied
offline. Filtering preceded ocular correction, so the independent component analysis was
trained on the same 0.1 Hz high-passed data that the analyses themselves use. Owing to a
processing oversight, the Session 3 recordings of four
participants (lab IDs 7, 8, 9 and 16) were high-pass filtered at 1 Hz rather than 0.1 Hz.
These four participant-sessions are excluded from every fitted ERP model and from the
decoding.`r misfilter_status()` They are retained in two places, both flagged where they
occur. The accuracy models draw on the behavioural record, which the filter setting does
not touch. The descriptive grand-average waveforms, difference waves and topographies
shown in the Results are extracted on the full sample, and their captions say so. The
exclusion rests on the filter setting itself, a documented generator of artefacts in this
kind of paradigm [@tanner2015; @widmann2015], and on nothing observed in these
participants' data, so the choice is not results-contingent. The argument is set out in
@apx-analytic-decisions-in-detail. `r misfilter_share_sentence()`
The pipeline can be re-run with them retained.^[The repository documents a
configuration switch that refits the ERP grid with the four datasets retained, so the
full-sample counterpart of every ERP estimate reported here is recoverable. The behavioural
models are unaffected, the offline filter bearing only on the EEG, and the decoding
artefacts carry no tag for the switch, so a full-sample decoding run has to be kept apart
from the reported one.] Ocular artefacts were then corrected by independent component
analysis, and the record was segmented into epochs from $-100$ to $1098$ ms relative to the
onset of the critical word. Trial-by-trial artefact rejection followed, retaining on
average `r erp_ret("mean")` of the 48 presented trials per modelled cell
($SD = `r erp_ret("sd")`$), a mean rejection rate of `r erp_ret("pct_discarded")`%.
These retention figures are computed on the full sample, as the grand averages are, so
the four mis-filtered Session 3 datasets contribute to the Session 3 means.
@tbl-retention-trials gives the full per-condition breakdown. Differential trial
loss between the compared conditions would make a grammaticality effect partly a difference
in measurement precision and only partly one in brain response, so retention is reported per
condition, and the two prove effectively equal.
Averaged over properties and sessions, `r ret_by_gram("Grammatical")` trials were retained
on grammatical trials and
`r ret_by_gram("Ungrammatical")` on ungrammatical trials, a difference of
`r ret_gram_gap()` trials.

For each retained trial, we computed the mean amplitude in three theoretically
motivated latency windows, 200--500 ms (the LAN/early-negativity range),
300--600 ms (the N400 range) and 400--900 ms (the P600 range), at lateral and
midline electrode macroregions. The windows are named by their nominal bounds
throughout. On the 2 ms acquisition grid, each is inclusive of samples up to
498, 598 and 898 ms respectively. That convention is inherited from the validated importer
and is noted here so that the figures and the code can be read against the prose. The lateral
region comprises left- and
right-hemisphere anterior, medial and posterior clusters and so carries both the
hemisphere and the caudality contrasts. The midline region comprises three clusters
centred on the midline and supports the caudality contrast alone. Those clusters are parasagittal, so they are
not strictly midline. Besides Fz, Cz, Pz and Oz they include the pairs
FC1/FC2 and CP1/CP2, which the cap places about a quarter of the head radius either
side of it. Because each pair is exactly symmetric, however, the cluster mean remains
centred on the midline and has no net hemispheric bias, which is why no hemisphere
term is estimated there. Two further choices, the within-participant $z$-scoring of
single-trial amplitudes and the treatment of each trial's pre-stimulus mean amplitude
($-100$ to $0$ ms) as a covariate instead of a subtracted baseline, are modelling
decisions and are set out under *Data analysis*.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-retention-trials
#| tbl-cap: "Retained Single-Trial EEG per Modelled Cell, by Grammatical Property and Session"
#| apa-note: "Values are mean trials retained of the 48 presented, averaged over language. Rows are split by grammaticality because differential trial loss across the compared conditions can bias both amplitude and decodability. The two conditions are retained almost equally here (see text). An n/a entry marks a session at which the property had not yet been introduced. Like the grand averages, the table is computed on the full sample, including the four mis-filtered Session 3 datasets that the models exclude."
if (!is.null(erp_ret_tbl) && has_knitr && "scope" %in% names(erp_ret_tbl)) {
  pc <- erp_ret_tbl[erp_ret_tbl$scope == "per_condition_canonical", , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(pc)) {
    # Factor (not character) so rows follow the order in which the properties were
    # introduced across sessions, rather than alphabetically.
    pc$Property <- factor(.table_props[match(pc$grammatical_property, names(.table_props))],
                          levels = unname(.table_props))
    # Retain grammaticality: averaging over it would remove the very comparison this
    # table exists to license, since differential trial loss between the compared
    # conditions would mean the grammaticality effect is partly a difference in
    # measurement precision rather than in brain response.
    pc$Condition <- factor(pc$grammaticality, levels = c("Grammatical", "Ungrammatical"))
    agg <- aggregate(mean_retained ~ Property + Condition + session, data = pc, FUN = mean)
    agg <- agg[order(agg$Property, agg$Condition), ]
    wide <- reshape(agg, idvar = c("Property", "Condition"), timevar = "session",
                    direction = "wide")
    names(wide) <- sub("^mean_retained\\.", "S", names(wide))
    # The NAs left by the reshape are structural: the property had not yet entered the
    # design at that session. Printing them as "NA" reads as missing data; an n/a entry
    # keeps the rendered table consistent with the note for a cell that could not exist.
    num <- vapply(wide, is.numeric, logical(1))
    wide[num] <- lapply(wide[num], function(x)
      ifelse(is.na(x), "n/a", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)))
    knitr::kable(wide, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "l", rep("r", sum(num))))
  } else cat("*Per-condition retention pending.*")
} else {
  cat("*Per-condition retention table will appear once `_erp_trial_retention.csv` is present.*")
}
```

## Grammaticality-judgement task

The grammaticality judgement was collected concurrently with the ERP recording. On
each experimental trial, participants judged whether the sentence was grammatical for
the property under test, so the trial-level accuracy (correct/incorrect) and the
single-trial ERP are two measures of one and the same event, recorded within a single
task. Accuracy is the sole behavioural dependent measure. Response times
served only to screen trials.
Judgements of `r rt_screen("rt_min_ms")` ms or less, or of `r rt_screen("rt_max_ms")`
ms or more, were discarded as implausible, which removed
`r rt_screen("n_rt_excluded")` of the `r rt_screen("n_valid_trials")` otherwise valid
judgement trials (`r rt_screen("pct_rt_excluded", 1)`%), leaving
`r rt_screen("n_kept")` trials for analysis. The bounds were carried over from the
legacy preprocessing pipeline, which recorded no rationale for them, so we disclose
the screen and its cost without defending the cutoffs. `r acc_gap_sentence()` Rows
that the presentation software logged twice under one trial number were reduced to one
per participant, session, property and trial, and the unlabelled filler sentences shown
at Session 2 carry no property and fall outside the modelled contrast. The judgement
sentences were generated combinatorially, which has a consequence for the accuracy
models' random-effect structure (see *Data analysis*).

## Data analysis

All models were fitted in a fully Bayesian framework with `brms` [@burkner2017;
@burkner2018] as a front end to the Stan No-U-Turn sampler [@carpenter2017]. A Bayesian
treatment is not incidental to the question here. The hypotheses concern the size and
direction of effects that are expected to be small. Several of the comparisons that
matter, such as whether a property's transfer effect grows across sessions, are naturally
expressed as statements about a posterior. Priors, sampler settings, diagnostics and
inference rules are set out in the sections that follow. The analysis and reporting code
was written with the assistance of Claude Code (version 2.1, Anthropic), running
primarily the Claude Opus and Claude Fable models, which drafted and revised scripts
under the authors' direction and checked them against the method reported here. The
authors reviewed and ran every script, and the deposited code reproduces the analyses
without the tool.

### Predictor coding and standardisation

Every continuous predictor was $z$-standardised and every dichotomous predictor
was $\pm 0.5$ contrast coded before model fitting (the $\pm 0.5$ codes are then
$z$-standardised with the other predictors, which preserves their sign). On this
common standardised scale, regression coefficients are directly comparable, and
lower-order terms in interactive models retain interpretable main-effect meanings
[@brauer2018; @schielzeth2010]. Standardising the inputs is also what makes a prior
on a coefficient interpretable, because it fixes the scale that prior is placed on
[@gelman2008]. Session was recoded to consecutive integers in the order the four
sessions occurred, Sessions 2, 3, 4 and 6 becoming 0--3, and then $z$-standardised
(within property for the accuracy models, whose properties span different session
ranges). The change in an effect between any two measured sessions,
including across the retention interval, is then a single linear combination of the
posterior draws. Besides grammaticality (grammatical $= +0.5$) and language
(Mini-Norwegian $= +0.5$), stated with the design, the topographic contrasts are
coded hemisphere right $= +0.5$, left $= -0.5$, and caudality anterior $= +0.5$,
medial $= 0$, posterior $= -0.5$. A positive coefficient on a topographic
interaction therefore indicates a larger effect over right or anterior sites respectively.

One further covariate enters the ERP models. It is the L1 Dominance Score, the
per-participant derived score of that name in the Language History Questionnaire's
Aggregate Scores export [LHQ3: @lhq3], read from that export and $z$-standardised with the
other continuous predictors. It indexes how far the first language dominates the
participant's repertoire, and it is carried in the ERP models as a control for prior
language experience. The variable is named for multilingual language diversity in the
extraction code, a legacy of an earlier version of the export in which the two scores sat
in different columns, so the code label and the quantity modelled differ; the models use
the score described here. The covariate is not carried into the accuracy models. That
asymmetry has no justification, and we return to it in the Limitations.

The response side has two standardisation decisions of its own. Single-trial
amplitudes were $z$-scored within participant. The reasoning is the one @faust1999
set out for response latencies. When individuals differ in the overall scale of a
measure, and those differences are roughly linear, a group whose scale is larger
will show a larger raw treatment effect, and the resulting overadditive interaction
is an artefact of scale. They recommend a within-individual $z$ transformation as
the remedy. Single-trial ERP amplitude has the same property, and the risk applies
directly here because the language contrast is between participants, so a scale
difference between the two groups could otherwise present as a grammaticality
$\times$ language interaction.
We also entered the trial's own
pre-stimulus mean amplitude ($-100$ to $0$ ms) as a within-participant $z$-scored
covariate. Subtraction of a baseline is the special case of this model in which the
baseline coefficient is fixed at one. Estimating that coefficient lets the model absorb
baseline variance that subtraction would leave in the residual, which @alday2019
shows can raise power. It also avoids the assumption subtraction requires, that conditions
do not differ systematically during the baseline interval.

### Model structure

For each ERP cell (property $\times$ window $\times$ macroregion), we fitted a
Gaussian model of single-trial mean amplitude:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{amplitude} \sim\; & \text{baseline} + \text{Gram} \times \text{Session} \times \text{Language} \\
 & + \text{Gram} \times \text{Hemisphere (lateral only)} + \text{Gram} \times \text{Caudality} \\
 & + \text{L1 dominance} \\
 & + (1 + \text{Gram} + \text{Session} \mid \text{participant}) + (1 + \text{Gram} + \text{Session} \mid \text{item}).
\end{aligned}
$$

For each property, we fitted a Bernoulli (logit-link) model of judgement accuracy
[@jaeger2008; @dixon2008]:
$$
\text{correct} \sim \text{Gram} \times \text{Session} \times \text{Language}
 + (1 + \text{Gram} + \text{Session} \mid \text{participant}).
$$

Participants and items are crossed rather than hierarchically nested. Within a
language, every participant sees every sentence frame, and every frame is seen by every
participant in that language, so the ERP models carry crossed by-participant and by-item
random effects [@baayen2008; @barr2013]. Items are nested within language, because the
two miniature languages draw on separate lexicons, so language does not vary within an
item and no by-item language slope is estimable. Grammaticality and session, by contrast,
vary within both grouping factors, since every frame is presented in both a grammatical
and an ungrammatical version and is re-presented across sessions.

Random effects therefore follow the "keep it maximal *as justified by the design*"
principle [@barr2013], so both grouping factors receive a random intercept plus
grammaticality and session slopes, with correlations estimated under the shared
$\mathrm{LKJ}(2)$ prior.

Session enters that specification as a single linear predictor, so the change in the
grammaticality effect across the retention interval is read off the fitted trend rather
than estimated for that interval on its own. Gender agreement and differential object
marking were therefore also refitted with a binary indicator for the retention session,
interacted with grammaticality and language and added to the linear session term. The
linear term then carries the training trend and the indicator the deviation at Session 6.
The indicator is coded $+0.5$ at Session 6 and $-0.5$ elsewhere and, unlike the other
predictors, is not standardised, so its coefficient is the deviation at Session 6 on the
response scale. The refits are otherwise identical to the models above and were run
under both random-effect structures. Verb--object number agreement admits no such refit. It is
sampled at the two bracketing sessions only, so an indicator for the later of them would
be collinear with the linear term. Where the two derivations disagree, the freed estimate
is the one that bears on consolidation, and both are reported (@tbl-retention,
@tbl-retention-free).

The case for retaining the by-item grammaticality slope, and the power-based argument
against maximal structures that it was weighed against [@barr2013; @matuschek2017], are
set out in @apx-analytic-decisions-in-detail. The Results report the whole grid refitted without that slope, so
a reader can see which conclusions depend on it. The accuracy models omit a by-item
effect by design. `r sentence_inventory_clause()` Item variance is therefore thinly
sampled per sentence, and no by-item term is carried. Its variance is absorbed into the
residual, which leaves the accuracy estimates slightly less precise and is noted under
*Limitations* [@barr2013].

### Priors

We placed informative priors derived from the
morphosyntactic-ERP and behavioural literature, in place of the common
weakly informative default, following a selective, sign-informed and
magnitude-regularising strategy [@schad2021]. Because the response and all predictors
are standardised, each coefficient is expressed in standard-deviation units (within
participant, for the ERP models). A prior *mean* can therefore encode the direction of a
well-established effect, while its *standard deviation* stays wide enough to let the data
dominate any well-identified effect [@gelman2008].

The one firmly established directional effect is the P600: words that violate the
syntactic structure of a sentence elicit a late positivity, larger for ungrammatical than
for grammatical sentences [@osterhout1992]. For morphosyntactic violations specifically,
that positivity is posterior and centroparietal, and it is obtained in native speakers
[@mueller2005; @mueller2007; @chen2007] and, once some proficiency has been reached, in
artificial-language learners [@morganshort2010; @morganshort2012]. A P600 also
arises to structural violations in implicit artificial-grammar learning, where the
sequences carry no morphology at all [@silva2017]. Because
grammaticality is coded grammatical $=+0.5$, this implies a *negative* prior mean on the
grammaticality slope in the P600 window, carried more mildly into the 300--600 ms window
for the two agreement properties, whose late signature is a positivity rather than an N400.
For differential object marking, the specification differs in both windows, being widened
in the later window and left zero-centred in the earlier one, because case-marking
violations are configuration-dependent and elicit a P600, an N400 or a biphasic response
according to animacy and markedness [@nieuwland2013; @frisch2001; @mueller2007]. As the P600 is
posterior-maximal [@mueller2007], the grammaticality $\times$ caudality interaction
received a positive prior mean in each window in which the grammaticality prior carried a
sign. The early (200--500 ms) anterior-negativity window and the hemisphere interaction
were left zero-centred, because the LAN is small and present in only roughly half of
participants and items, so its sign is not safely predictable [@caffarra2019]. The grammaticality
$\times$ session $\times$ language transfer interaction, the hypothesis under test, was
kept zero-centred, because the second-language signature of these effects is qualitatively
contested [@chen2007; @mueller2009] and proficiency-dependent [@caffarra2015]. The priors
thus inform the model where the evidence is strong without biasing the effects we set out
to estimate.

For the accuracy models, artificial-language learners judge grammaticality well above
chance and improve across successive test blocks even under mere exposure, without
explicit instruction or feedback [@mueller2009], motivating a positive intercept and a
positive session slope. Random-effect standard deviations, and the residual standard
deviation of the ERP models, received a generous half--Student-$t$ prior, a weakly
informative default for variance parameters in hierarchical models [@gelman2006].
@tbl-priors in @apx-prior-specifications gives the distribution placed on every parameter. A generous prior is warranted here because between-participant variation in
the morphosyntactic ERP response is not incidental noise. @tanner2014 found that although
the grand mean showed the usual biphasic LAN--P600 pattern, individual responses varied
systematically along a continuum between negativity-dominant and positivity-dominant, so
participants differ in the form of the response and not only in its size. Modelling that
variation as a random effect over single trials, instead of averaging across it, is the
approach @volpertesmond2021 set out for ERP data. Random-effect correlation
matrices received an $\mathrm{LKJ}(2)$ prior [@lewandowski2009]. The literature does not
supply a defensible microvolt effect size for these components (even systematic resampling
finds the magnitude of the P600 to vary widely across samples, @kim2024).
Prior means therefore encode only sign and a regularised magnitude, and their influence is
bounded by deliberately wide standard deviations. Prior
predictive simulation confirmed that the priors imply amplitude and accuracy distributions
that encompass the observed data (@fig-priorpc). Every model in the grid, under both
random-effect structures, and every accuracy model was also refitted on the same data,
as a sensitivity analysis, under the former weakly informative priors of
$\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $\mathcal{N}(0, 1.5)$, and the estimates were essentially
unchanged.`r retfree_weak_note()` The largest
shift in any grammaticality term was `r prior_shift_max()` on the within-participant
standardised scale for the ERP models and `r prior_shift_max(family = "^accuracy_")` in
log-odds for the accuracy models. No grammaticality term's credible interval changed
width by more than `r prior_width_dev()`% in the ERP models or
`r prior_width_dev(family = "^accuracy_")`% in the accuracy models. Taken over every
reported parameter, the largest width change
was `r prior_width_dev(pattern = "", family = "")`%. The informative priors therefore regularise without driving the
conclusions [@schad2021; @depaoli2017; @vandeschoot2021]. The smallest of the credible
transfer effects (differential object marking, late lateral window) is unchanged under the
weak priors
(`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_400_900_lateral_weakprior_itemslope", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`),
so its credibility does not depend on them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-priorpc
#| fig-cap: "Prior Predictive Check for a Representative Model"
#| apa-note: "The model is subject--verb gender agreement, 400--900 ms midline. Light lines are datasets simulated from the priors alone, with the likelihood switched off, and the dark line is the observed within-participant z-scored single-trial amplitudes. The prior predictive distribution comfortably encompasses the observed data, so the priors are not in conflict with it. The horizontal axis spans the full range of the prior draws, which reach far beyond the observed range. That is the intended behaviour of wide priors on a standardised scale, and it is why the observed density appears compressed near zero. The check therefore establishes that the priors generate data of a plausible order of magnitude, not that they are tightly calibrated to the observed distribution."
#| out-width: "72%"
.ppc <- here::here("paper_1_transfer", "figures", "prior_predictive_check.png")
# Without the else branch, a checkout that lacks the PNG emits nothing at all and the
# cross-reference in the text above renders as a dangling "?@fig-priorpc".
if (file.exists(.ppc)) {
  knitr::include_graphics(.ppc)
} else {
  ggplot() + theme_void() +
    annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0,
             label = "Prior predictive check pending figure generation") +
    theme(plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20))
}
```

### Sampler settings and convergence

Each model was run with four chains of 10,000 iterations, the first 2,000 of each
discarded as warm-up, with `adapt_delta = 0.95` and `max_treedepth = 12` to accommodate the
challenging geometry of maximal multilevel posteriors. Convergence was assessed
with the rank-normalised split-$\widehat{R}$ and bulk/tail effective sample sizes
[@vehtari2021], requiring $\widehat{R} < 1.01$, bulk- and tail-ESS $> 400$, and
no divergent transitions. Model fit was checked with posterior predictive checks
[@gabry2019]. These two thresholds do different jobs. An
effective sample size of 400 (at least 100 per chain) is the point at which the
$\widehat{R}$ and ESS diagnostics are themselves reliable [@vehtari2021]. The stability of a
95% interval limit is a more demanding requirement, because extreme quantiles are estimated
far less efficiently than a posterior mean [@kruschke2021]. The realised sampling is
substantially above these thresholds (the lowest bulk- and tail-ESS over all parameters of
all models are reported in @tbl-convergence-appendix in @apx-convergence-diagnostics).
Coefficients whose intervals lie close to zero should nonetheless be treated as
borderline.

### Inference

We summarise each effect by its posterior median, 95% credible interval (CrI) and
probability of direction ($p_d$, the posterior probability that the effect has its
median's sign), an estimation-first approach that avoids dichotomous
null-hypothesis testing [@makowski2019]. We describe an effect as *credible* when its 95%
credible interval excludes zero, and otherwise read $p_d$ as a continuous index of
directional certainty [@kruschke2018]. All
credible intervals are equal-tailed quantile intervals bounded by the 2.5th and 97.5th
percentiles of the posterior draws. For a skewed
posterior, an equal-tailed and a highest-density interval can differ in whether they
contain zero, so the choice is stated [@kruschke2021]. Within each model, hierarchical shrinkage
across participants and items already regularises the coefficient estimates
[@kruschke2018; @gelmanhillyajima2012]. The eighteen cells are fitted separately and are
not pooled towards one another, so that shrinkage is not itself an argument about the grid. The grid (3
properties $\times$ 3 a priori windows $\times$ 2 macroregions) is fixed before
fitting, and every cell is reported without selection (@fig-erp-forest reports all 18
cells for the key terms, and @tbl-retention the derived retention contrasts). No
correction across cells is applied, and no cell is screened for significance before
being reported. Where a
conclusion does rest on particular cells crossing the credibility threshold (the
transfer interactions are credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`
cells), we treat it as provisional on that basis (see *Strength of evidence* in the
Discussion). We do not claim the grid is immune to selection effects [@rubin2021].
The derived retention effect (Session 4 $\to$
Session 6) and its language-scoped contrasts are posterior quantities computed from
the same models, summarised and disclosed in full the same way (@tbl-retention). For
gender agreement and differential object marking, they are also re-estimated in refits that
free the Session-6 step from the training trend, described under *Model structure*
(@tbl-retention-free).

### Multivariate decoding of grammaticality

The Bayesian models above summarise each electrode cluster's mean amplitude
separately, which could miss a grammaticality signal that is distributed across the
scalp too weakly to move any single cluster's mean but is nonetheless jointly
decodable from the whole-scalp pattern [@haxby2001]. As a complementary,
classical (non-Bayesian) analysis, we decoded Grammatical from
Ungrammatical trials directly from the single-trial amplitude pattern across all
EEG sensors at every time sample (baseline-corrected, downsampled to a 4 ms grid).
The classifier was a
regularised linear discriminant analysis under leave-one-participant-out
cross-validation, a time-resolved multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA)
approach for EEG/MEG [@grootswagers2017]. Leave-one-participant-out is the
generalisation test this question calls for, since what is at stake is whether the
pattern transfers to an unseen learner. @varoquaux2017 show that leave-one-out
schemes give more variable accuracy estimates than repeated random splits, so we read
the AUC time-course below as a profile whose individual point estimates carry limited
precision. Decoding performance is
summarised as the area under the ROC curve (AUC) at each time point. Chance-level
calibration was established with a permutation test that shuffles the
grammaticality labels once per permutation, holding the shuffle constant across the
whole time-course so that the null preserves each trial's temporal autocorrelation.
Multiple comparisons across time points were corrected with cluster-based
permutation inference [@maris2007]. Clusters were formed from temporally contiguous
samples whose AUC exceeded the 95th percentile of the pooled permutation null, the
cluster statistic was the summed excess of AUC over that threshold, and each cluster
was assessed against the distribution of the largest cluster statistic across
permutations. A second correction layer controls the false-discovery
rate (FDR) across clusters, with the family defined per property. Benjamini--Hochberg
correction ($q < .05$) is applied across the clusters of a
property's pooled overall time-course, and each property's family is corrected
separately. The session-resolved and session-by-language breakdowns carry only their own
cluster-level $p$ values. @apx-analytic-decisions-in-detail sets out why the family is defined this way.
Grammatical and ungrammatical trial counts differ
across participants and decline across sessions, so we balanced the classes by
undersampling the majority class within each participant of the training fold. The
discriminant's pooled within-class covariance was ridged by one thousandth of its mean
diagonal for numerical stability. The AUC is in any case insensitive to class
prevalence, so neither the classifier nor the metric can exploit a prevalence
shortcut, and chance was set by the empirical within-participant permutation null
[@combrisson2015]. The
permutation null comprised `r n_perm_txt()` shufflings, so the smallest attainable cluster
$p$ is `r min_cluster_p()`. This bounds the resolution of near-threshold cluster $p$-values,
and the surviving clusters are reported with that granularity in mind [@nichols2002;
@phipson2010].`r decode_status_method()` The
decoder is given the EEG sensors alone. The amplifier's built-in accelerometer
channels are excluded, as is any channel not exported for every session a property
was recorded in, so that each property's pattern is brain-derived and no sensor is
present for one session's trials but structurally absent for another's. Beyond the overall time-course, five further analyses were run. Decoding separately
by session, and by session $\times$ mini-language, gives a multivariate analogue of
the ERP models' grammaticality $\times$ session and $\times$ language terms. A
cross-language generalisation analysis trains the decoder on one mini-language and
tests it on the other. A cross-property generalisation analysis trains on one grammatical
property's Grammatical/Ungrammatical contrast and tests on another. Finally, temporal generalisation trains a decoder at every time
point and tests it at every other, on a grid coarsened by a factor of two on both axes to
keep the computation tractable. It characterises whether the same neural code is
stable across the epoch or evolves [@king2014]. The two generalisation analyses carry no
permutation null and are reported as descriptive comparisons. Cross-validating strictly
out-of-participant throughout guards against the circular, non-independent analysis
that would otherwise inflate apparent decoding accuracy [@kriegeskorte2009].

## Transparency, preregistration and analysis status

The study design, artificial-language materials and session protocol were
preregistered before data collection (<https://osf.io/tjr54>). The preregistration
specified the design, the miniature-language materials, the six-session schedule and
the EEG acquisition, but it did not commit to a statistical analysis plan. The
Bayesian multilevel models, the literature-derived informative priors, the latency
windows and macroregions, the Session 4 $\to$ 6 retention contrasts and the
multivariate decoding analyses reported here were therefore specified after the data
were collected. None was preregistered, so all are exploratory in the registered
sense, and we report them as estimation-oriented analyses, since none tests a
preregistered hypothesis [@nosek2018; @wagenmakers2012]. Within that frame,
we distinguish *primary* from *secondary* analyses. The primary analyses, fixed
before any model was fitted, comprise the ERP grid of properties, windows,
macroregions and priors together with the pooled, all-sessions decoding time-course
for each property. The secondary analyses are the session-resolved and
session-by-language decoding breakdowns, the cross-language and cross-property
generalisation analyses, and the temporal-generalisation matrix. What the
paper reports of them varies, and we say which is which. The cross-language and
cross-property peaks are quoted in the Results. The session-resolved and
session-by-language breakdowns and the temporal-generalisation matrices are not summarised
numerically here and are available in the deposited decoding artefacts. Where a secondary
analysis carries a cluster-level $p$ value, that value is family-wise-error-controlled over
time in the usual way, but none of them is treated as a test of the paper's claims. Where the decoding analyses
speak of a "confirmatory family", the term names the false-discovery-rate correction
family (the clusters of each property's pooled overall time-course), not
preregistered confirmation. On a minor point of adherence, a third, ancillary violation
type was recorded per property but, as noted above, is not analysed here.

Two decisions were made after inspecting results, and we label them as such. First, peak
decoding accuracies are quoted on the post-stimulus axis, a restriction adopted once the
pre-stimulus interval was found not to be at chance for differential object marking. The
pre-stimulus interval is retained and reported alongside as a negative control.
Second, the temporal-generalisation and cross-property analyses were reclassified as
descriptive after it became clear that no null distribution had been computed for them.
Neither decision creates a new test, and both move the reported result in the
conservative direction.`r decode_status_transparency()`

The preregistration planned data collection at two sites, in Norway and Spain. The
present analyses concern only the Norwegian cohort (first-language Norwegian,
second-language English learners of Mini-English or Mini-Norwegian). The Spanish-site
data are not analysed here. The findings therefore speak to
first-language-Norwegian learners, and generalisation to the other registered
populations is an open question.

Following the preregistered protocol, in each grammar session, participants had to
score above 80% on the post-training behavioural test (with a second attempt allowed)
before proceeding to the EEG experiment. This performance threshold is both an
inclusion criterion and a performance-conditional missingness mechanism, since it
conditions which participant-sessions contribute EEG and behaviour. Its effect is
therefore folded into the attendance counts in @fig-flow, which record who contributed
data at each stage but not why. Per-session gate outcomes are not reported. They can only
be reconstructed from the terminal pass flag in the training logs, and that reconstruction
does not reconcile with the attendance counts at Session 4, so we do not quote numbers
from it.

# Results

```{r}
#| results: asis
# Convergence is reported as a worst case in one sentence rather than as a table of one
# row per fit. The population is 18 ERP cells under two random-effect structures and two
# prior sets (72), plus 3 accuracy models -- which have a single structure, since no
# by-item term is identifiable for them -- under the two prior sets (6), plus the
# retention-free refits of the 12 gender-agreement and differential-object-marking cells
# under both structures with the informative priors (24). Every one meets the criteria,
# so the table would be that many rows of near-identical numbers and two columns that
# never varied. The extreme value over all of them carries the same information: if the
# worst R-hat is below the threshold then so is every other. The per-model values remain
# available in @tbl-convergence-appendix. The count is taken from the artefact rather
# than typed, so it cannot drift when the grid is extended (as it was by the refits).
if (!is.null(conv_tbl)) {
  np <- sum(conv_tbl$passed, na.rm = TRUE)
  n_fit <- nrow(conv_tbl)
  # Only claim "all" when all of them passed; otherwise state the proportion, so a single
  # failing refit cannot render as "All N met the criteria. 1 model did not meet it."
  cat(sprintf(paste0(
    "%s met the convergence criteria. Taken over every parameter of every ",
    "model, the largest rank-normalised $\\widehat{R}$ was %.3f, the smallest bulk and ",
    "tail effective sample sizes were %s and %s, and no model produced a divergent ",
    "transition. Per-model values are given in @tbl-convergence-appendix.\n"),
    if (np == n_fit) sprintf("All %d fitted models", n_fit)
    else sprintf("%d of the %d fitted models", np, n_fit),
    max(conv_tbl$max_rhat, na.rm = TRUE),
    format(round(min(conv_tbl$min_ess_bulk, na.rm = TRUE)), big.mark = ","),
    format(round(min(conv_tbl$min_ess_tail, na.rm = TRUE)), big.mark = ",")))
  if (np < n_fit) {
    cat(sprintf(" The remaining %s identified in the table in the convergence appendix.\n",
                if (n_fit - np == 1L) "model is" else sprintf("%d models are", n_fit - np)))
  }
} else {
  cat("*Convergence diagnostics will appear here once the models are fitted.*\n")
}
```

## ERP signatures of grammatical processing and their development

We assess, for each property, whether it elicited a grammaticality effect, whether that
effect sharpened across sessions (the grammaticality $\times$ session interaction), and
whether that development was modulated by language (the grammaticality $\times$ session
$\times$ language interaction). The overall pattern is property-specific, with gender
agreement showing the clearest and most broadly distributed learning effect, credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", "gender_agreement")` cells;
verb--object number agreement a late, language-conditioned effect; and differential object
marking a transient early grammaticality effect with a late, language-conditioned
modulation (@fig-erp-forest). The underlying condition averages are shown as
grand-average waveforms in @fig-erp-waveforms. Because those overlaid waveforms are
dominated by the shared evoked response, the difference waves that isolate the
grammaticality effect are given in @apx-difference-waves (@fig-erp-difference).

One coding fact governs how every coefficient below should be read. A positive
grammaticality coefficient means that grammatical trials were more positive than
ungrammatical ones, because grammaticality is coded grammatical $= +0.5$. Violations
therefore appear as a relative negativity. The canonical P600 would produce a negative
coefficient. Every credible grammaticality effect below is positive, so the dominant
signature in these learners is a violation-related negativity where our priors
anticipated a late positivity, a point we return to in the Discussion. Results are
organised by property.

```{r}
#| label: fig-erp-forest
#| fig-cap: "Posterior Medians and 95% Credible Intervals for the Key Standardised Effects Across ERP Cells"
#| apa-note: "Cells are arranged by grammatical property (rows) and term (columns), with each cell's window and macroregion on the vertical axis. All panels share a common x axis, so effect magnitudes are directly comparable across cells and terms. Filled points mark effects whose 95% interval excludes zero; open points do not. Estimates are in within-participant SD units."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 7
# Height is 7in, not the 9in used previously: at 9 the panel plus this caption overran
# the APA text block, so the shared x axis -- the scale the caption tells the reader to
# compare magnitudes across -- was pushed off the bottom of the page entirely.
key_terms <- c("z_recoded_grammaticality",
               "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session",
               "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")
if (results_ready) {
  prop_lab <- LES_PROPERTY_LABELS
  win_ord  <- c("200-500 ms", "300-600 ms", "400-900 ms")
  # Keep ONE fit per cell. post_tbl holds four variants of every cell -- the base and
  # maximal random-effect structures crossed with the informative and weak prior sets --
  # and without this filter all four were drawn at the same coordinates, so the figure
  # superimposed the reported fits on the sensitivity fits: 216 point-ranges where there
  # should be 54, with no way to tell which was which. Route through .mid() so the figure
  # follows LES_P1_PRIMARY rather than naming a structure here.
  fp <- post_tbl |>
    filter(parameter %in% key_terms, !startsWith(model, "accuracy_"),
           !grepl("_weakprior", model),
           model == vapply(sub("_itemslope$", "", model), .mid, "")) |>
    mutate(
      Term   = factor(.pretty_term(parameter), levels = .pretty_term(key_terms)),
      # Strip the structure suffix before parsing. The filter above keeps the primary
      # structure's ids, which under LES_P1_PRIMARY = "maximal" all end "_itemslope";
      # the Region/Window/Prop patterns below anchor on a "(lateral|midline)$" ending,
      # so parsing the suffixed id returns it unchanged and every label becomes NA.
      id     = sub("_itemslope$", "", gsub("^erp_", "", model)),
      Region = c(lateral = "Lateral", midline = "Midline")[sub(".*_(lateral|midline)$", "\\1", id)],
      Window = factor(sub(".*_([0-9]+)_([0-9]+)_(lateral|midline)$", "\\1-\\2 ms", id), levels = win_ord),
      Prop   = factor(unname(prop_lab[sub("_[0-9]+_[0-9]+_(lateral|midline)$", "", id)]),
                      levels = unname(prop_lab)),
      Row    = paste0(Window, ", ", Region),
      Credible = (ci_low > 0) | (ci_high < 0))
  if (nrow(fp)) {
    fp <- fp[order(fp$Region, fp$Window), ]
    fp$Row <- factor(fp$Row, levels = rev(unique(fp$Row)))
    ggplot(fp, aes(x = median, y = Row)) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
      geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high, shape = Credible)) +
      facet_grid(Prop ~ Term, labeller = label_wrap_gen(16)) +
      scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 1, `TRUE` = 16), guide = "none") +
      labs(x = "Posterior estimate (within-participant SD units)", y = NULL) +
      les_theme() +
      theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
  } else {
    ggplot() + theme_void() + ggtitle("No ERP posterior summaries found.")
  }
} else {
  ggplot() + theme_void() +
    annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "ERP forest plot pending model fit") +
    theme(plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-erp-waveforms
#| fig-cap: "Grand-Average ERPs per Property at Two Representative Sites"
#| apa-note: "Waveforms are shown at a midline posterior region (parieto-occipital, spanning the P600) and a left-anterior region (spanning the LAN/early negativity), grammatical against ungrammatical. Each line is the mean over all retained trials of all contributing participants, so participants with more retained trials contribute more to the mean. Positive voltage is plotted upward. Time zero is critical-word onset, and the pre-stimulus baseline ($-100$ to 0 ms) is shaded. The vertical axis is scaled separately for the two sites. The waveforms are not baseline-corrected (the single-trial models use each trial's own pre-stimulus baseline). The three a priori analysis windows (200--500, 300--600 and 400--900 ms) are shaded. They overlap by design, because the underlying components do, so the depth of shading reflects window overlap and does not mark out any one window. These are descriptive condition averages with no uncertainty band, and the inferential statements come from the models in the forest plot. Unlike those models, they are computed on the full sample, including the four mis-filtered Session-3 datasets described in the Method."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5
# Sorted in byte order so the row order of the pooled frame does not depend on the
# collation of the rendering machine.
ga_files <- sort(list.files(paper1_results(), pattern = "^_grand_average_.*\\.csv$",
                            full.names = TRUE), method = "radix")
.props3 <- unname(LES_PROPERTY_LABELS)
if (length(ga_files) >= 6) {
  ga <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ga_files, utils::read.csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
  reps <- c("midline posterior", "left anterior")
  gw <- ga[ga$brain_region %in% reps, ]
  gw$Site <- factor(gw$brain_region, levels = reps,
                    labels = c("Midline posterior", "Left anterior"))
  gw$Property <- factor(gw$grammatical_property, levels = .props3)
  ggplot(gw, aes(time, mean_amp, colour = grammaticality)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -100, xmax = 0, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.35) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 200, xmax = 498, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.05, fill = "grey40") +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 300, xmax = 598, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.05, fill = "grey40") +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 400, xmax = 898, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.09, fill = "grey40") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey55") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey55") +
    geom_line(aes(linetype = grammaticality), linewidth = 0.5) +
    facet_grid(Site ~ Property, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Grammatical = "#000000", Ungrammatical = "#D55E00")) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Grammatical = "solid", Ungrammatical = "22")) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000)) +
    labs(x = "Time from critical-word onset (ms)",
         y = expression("Mean amplitude (" * mu * "V, positive up)"),
         colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
    les_theme() + theme(legend.position = "top")
} else {
  ggplot() + theme_void() + ggtitle("Grand-average waveforms pending extraction")
}
```

### Subject--verb gender agreement

Gender agreement showed the clearest profile. The grammaticality effect was positive in
direction in every window and macroregion ($p_d$ from
`r pd_range("z_recoded_grammaticality", "^erp_gender_agreement", sep = "to")`;
@fig-erp-forest) and credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality", "gender_agreement")` cells, both of them on the
midline`r cred_cells_guard("z_recoded_grammaticality", c("erp_gender_agreement_200_500_midline", "erp_gender_agreement_300_600_midline"), "gender_agreement")`.
Laterally, the intervals include zero throughout. The effect also sharpened across
sessions, and that development is the better supported of the two. The
grammaticality $\times$ session interaction was credible from the early window (lateral
200--500 ms, `r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_200_500_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`; midline 300--600 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_300_600_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`) through the late window (midline 400--900 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`). Source-language transfer in the ERP signal was
not credible, however. The grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language interaction sat
near zero in the late window (`r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`), with only an
early-window hint (midline 200--500 ms, `r report_effect("erp_gender_agreement_200_500_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`).

### Differential object marking

Differential object marking showed an early, transient grammaticality effect (grammatical
trials more positive, a relative violation negativity), and no developing late
effect. The effect was credible in the early midline window alone
(@fig-erp-forest; 200--500 ms, `r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`), with its
lateral counterpart positive but not credible
(`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`), and was, if anything, slightly negative by the late window
(midline 400--900 ms, `r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`). One caveat
attaches to this early effect specifically. Because the violation omits the particle
*fi*, the two conditions differ physically in the region preceding the critical word. At
the roughly 505 ms word-onset asynchrony, the response to that region overlaps the
200--500 ms window of the critical epoch. The same low-level difference that renders the
pre-stimulus decoding baseline non-chance (see below) could therefore contribute here, so
we read the early effect as a violation-related response with a possible stimulus-driven
component. Its development was not credible
(`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`), but the grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language
transfer interaction was credible in the two later lateral windows (300--600 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_300_600_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`;
400--900 ms, `r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_400_900_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`).
The effect carried the same negative sign (a development smaller for the Mini-Norwegian
group, given the coding above) in all six cells and did not reach credibility on
the midline (400--900 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`), so it
forms a coherent lateral, late-window pattern that spans several cells. Its sign is
opposite to the verb--object transfer effect reported next, so the two properties diverge
in direction as well as in magnitude.

### Verb--object number agreement

Verb--object number agreement, the latest-introduced property, developed only in the late
window (@fig-erp-forest), and there it bore a source-language signal. The grammaticality $\times$ session
interaction was credible laterally (400--900 ms, `r report_effect("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`), as was the
grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language transfer interaction
(`r report_effect("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`). On the midline,
the same interaction was not credible
(`r report_effect("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_midline", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`). The lateral effect
is the only positive one among the `r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`
cells in which a transfer interaction is credible, and every one of those cells is
lateral`r cred_cells_guard("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", c("erp_differential_object_marking_300_600_lateral", "erp_differential_object_marking_400_900_lateral", "erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_lateral"))`.
Midline intervals are wider throughout the grid because the three midline clusters
supply half as many observations as the six lateral ones.

One reading caveat applies to this property alone. Verb--object number agreement is
measured at Sessions 4 and 6 only, and the interval between them is the unrehearsed
retention gap, so for this property the session term is the change across that gap and
contains no further exposure. Its grammaticality $\times$ session and three-way terms are
therefore offline-interval changes, and the *learning* and *transfer* glosses that the
operationalisation gives those terms for the other two properties do not carry over
unaltered here. We read them accordingly throughout.

### Topography

Grammaticality interacted with hemisphere for differential object marking (200--500 ms,
`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_200_500_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_hemisphere")`),
the effect being larger over the right hemisphere (hemisphere is coded right $= +0.5$).
The priors were neutral on this asymmetry (zero-centred, because the one lateralised
component is too heterogeneous to sign a priori), so nothing about it was predicted, and
no by-participant slope was estimated for it. The
grammaticality $\times$ caudality interaction, by contrast, was not credible in the late
window for any property (all $p_d$ between
`r pd_range("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_caudality", "^erp_.*400_900")`). Raw
voltage varies with anterior--posterior position, as it does across any scalp
recording, but the grammaticality effect itself was no more pronounced posteriorly than
anteriorly, so the topography does not confirm a canonical posterior-maximal P600
distribution (@fig-erp-topography).

```{r}
#| label: fig-erp-topography
#| fig-cap: "Scalp Topography of the Grammaticality Effect in the 400--900 ms Window, per Property"
#| apa-note: "The topography is the grammatical minus ungrammatical mean amplitude, averaged over all retained trials and so weighted by each participant's retained-trial count, with no baseline correction. As with the waveforms, the average is taken over the full sample, including the four mis-filtered Session-3 datasets that the models exclude. The field is interpolated by thin-plate spline across the 30 electrodes assigned to the analysis regions (dots; nose at the top) and masked to the head, so no value is shown for scalp the montage did not sample. Sensor positions are the study's own recorded montage, read from the BrainVision headers. The outline marks the equator, and ears are drawn for orientation. The two low-temporal sites that sit below the equator (FT9/FT10) therefore fall outside the outline and are drawn as open circles. They inform the interpolation at the rim but no value is plotted beyond the equator. Warmer values indicate a larger grammatical-trial amplitude. The colour scale is symmetric about zero and shared across properties, and the grey line is the zero contour, so the sign of a region can be read without the colour. The distribution is diffuse and not posterior-maximal, consistent with the model-based grammaticality-by-caudality interaction not being credible for any property in this window (see main text)."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 2.1
elec_ga_files <- sort(list.files(paper1_results(), pattern = "^_electrode_grand_average_.*\\.csv$",
                                 full.names = TRUE), method = "radix")
elec_xy <- .read_csv_if(paper1_results("_electrode_coordinates.csv"))
if (length(elec_ga_files) >= 6 && !is.null(elec_xy) && requireNamespace("mgcv", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ega <- do.call(rbind, lapply(elec_ga_files, utils::read.csv, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
  eagg <- ega[ega$time >= 400 & ega$time <= 898, ] |>
    dplyr::group_by(grammatical_property, grammaticality, electrode) |>
    dplyr::summarise(a = mean(mean_amp, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  eg <- dplyr::rename(dplyr::filter(eagg, grammaticality == "Grammatical"),   gram = a)
  eu <- dplyr::rename(dplyr::filter(eagg, grammaticality == "Ungrammatical"), ungram = a)
  ed <- dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(eg, -grammaticality), dplyr::select(eu, -grammaticality),
                         by = c("grammatical_property", "electrode"))
  ed$diff <- ed$gram - ed$ungram
  ed <- dplyr::left_join(ed, elec_xy[, c("electrode", "x", "y")], by = "electrode")
  ed <- ed[!is.na(ed$x) & !is.na(ed$diff), ]

  # The head outline is the equator, which the montage's projection places at radius 1
  # (derive it from the sensors that are 90 degrees from the vertex rather than assuming).
  # FT9/FT10 sit below the equator and so fall just outside the outline; they still
  # inform the interpolation at the rim. The map is masked to the head, so no value is
  # shown for scalp the montage never measured.
  R  <- mean(sqrt(elec_xy$x^2 + elec_xy$y^2)[abs(elec_xy$theta) == 90])
  gr <- expand.grid(x = seq(-R, R, length.out = 130), y = seq(-R, R, length.out = 130))
  gr <- gr[sqrt(gr$x^2 + gr$y^2) <= R, ]
  interp_one <- function(dd) {
    m <- tryCatch(mgcv::gam(diff ~ s(x, y, k = 20), data = dd, method = "REML"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
    out <- gr
    out$diff <- as.numeric(stats::predict(m, newdata = gr))
    out$grammatical_property <- dd$grammatical_property[1]
    out
  }
  surf <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(ed, ed$grammatical_property), interp_one))
  if (!is.null(surf) && nrow(surf)) {
    surf$Property <- factor(surf$grammatical_property, levels = .props3)
    ed$Property   <- factor(ed$grammatical_property, levels = .props3)
    lim  <- max(abs(surf$diff), na.rm = TRUE)
    tt   <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 240)
    head_outline <- data.frame(x = R * cos(tt), y = R * sin(tt))
    nose <- data.frame(x = c(-0.13 * R, 0, 0.13 * R), y = c(0.985 * R, 1.12 * R, 0.985 * R))
    # Ears. Without them the two low-temporal sensors (FT9/FT10), which sit below the
    # equator and so outside the outline, read as stray marks rather than as electrodes
    # in an anatomically sensible position.
    ea <- seq(-pi / 2.6, pi / 2.6, length.out = 60)
    ear_r <- function(side) data.frame(
      x = side * (R * cos(ea) * 0.10 + R * 0.995),
      y = R * sin(ea) * 0.19)
    ggplot(surf, aes(x, y)) +
      geom_tile(aes(fill = diff)) +
      # The zero contour carries the sign of the difference as a second cue, so the map
      # survives greyscale printing, where the two ends of the diverging scale are
      # close in luminance.
      geom_contour(aes(z = diff), breaks = 0, colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.3) +
      geom_path(data = head_outline, aes(x, y), colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
      geom_path(data = nose, aes(x, y), colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
      geom_path(data = ear_r(1),  aes(x, y), colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
      geom_path(data = ear_r(-1), aes(x, y), colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
      # Sensors inside the plotted equator are filled; the two low-temporal sites that
      # sit below it (FT9/FT10) are drawn as open circles, so they read as deliberately
      # placed electrodes outside the outline rather than as stray marks.
      geom_point(data = ed[sqrt(ed$x^2 + ed$y^2) <= R + 1e-9, ], aes(x, y),
                 size = 0.7, colour = "grey15") +
      geom_point(data = ed[sqrt(ed$x^2 + ed$y^2) >  R + 1e-9, ], aes(x, y),
                 size = 0.9, shape = 1, stroke = 0.3, colour = "grey45") +
      facet_wrap(~ Property) +
      scale_fill_gradient2(low = les_div[1], mid = les_div[2], high = les_div[3],
                           midpoint = 0, limits = c(-lim, lim)) +
      coord_fixed(clip = "off") +
      labs(fill = expression(atop("Grammatical -", "ungrammatical (" * mu * "V)"))) +
      theme_void(base_size = LES_FIG_BASE_SIZE) +
      theme(legend.position = "right", plot.margin = margin(0, 4, 4, 4))
  }
} else {
  ggplot() + theme_void() + ggtitle("Scalp topography pending per-electrode extraction")
}
```

### Dependence on the by-item random-effect structure

Everything above comes from the maximal structure, with crossed by-participant and
by-item random effects each carrying a grammaticality slope. Refitting the whole grid
without the by-item grammaticality slope leaves every transfer conclusion unchanged
(`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", structure = "itemslope")`
credible cells against
