`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", structure = "base")`)
but narrows the grammaticality main effect's intervals by about
`r itemslope_width_ratio("z_recoded_grammaticality")` times, so the breadth of that
effect across cells is structure-dependent while its existence and direction hold under
both. The comparison is set out in full in @apx-analytic-decisions-in-detail.

## Retention (Session 4 to Session 6)

The retention contrast quantifies the change in the grammaticality effect between Sessions
4 and 6, positive values indicating an effect that strengthened over the interval and
values near zero an effect that held steady. Its derivation bounds what it can show. Session
enters the models as a single linear predictor, so the contrast is the per-session change
in the grammaticality effect rescaled to the width of the retention step. Every session in
the series informs that estimate, including those outside the retention interval. For
gender agreement, sampled from Session 2, and for differential object marking, sampled
from Session 3, the contrast describes the fitted trajectory evaluated over the retention
interval. It cannot by itself separate an offline gain specific to that interval
from continued improvement at the rate the training sessions established. Verb--object
number agreement is the exception, being present at Sessions 4 and 6 only, so for that
property the linear session term is precisely the change across those two sessions and the
contrast is estimated directly from them. @tbl-retention, in @apx-retention-tables,
reports every contrast overall, within each language and, where derived, as the
between-language difference; the text below reports the ones that carry the argument.

For gender agreement and differential object marking, that limitation is addressed
directly. Both properties were refitted with an indicator for the retention session,
interacted with grammaticality and language, so that the linear term carries the training
trend and the indicator the deviation at Session 6. @tbl-retention-free, in the same
appendix, reports those freed contrasts. They answer a different question from @tbl-retention, and where the two
disagree, the freed estimate is the one that bears on consolidation. Verb--object number
agreement admits no such refit, for the reason given under *Model structure*.

The retention contrasts reveal a property- and language-specific pattern. The
gender-agreement grammaticality effect strengthened across the interval, credibly and in
both languages (midline 400--900 ms, `r report_contrast("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline", "overall")`). Verb--object number agreement
strengthened overall (lateral 400--900 ms,
`r report_contrast("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_lateral", "overall")`), but
that gain was carried by the Mini-Norwegian group
(`r report_contrast("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_lateral", "within_Mini-Norwegian")`; Mini-English `r report_contrast("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_lateral", "within_Mini-English")`), and the
difference between the languages is itself credible
(`r report_contrast("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_lateral", "language_difference")`).
Differential object marking showed no credible overall ERP retention in any cell, but its
grammaticality effect strengthened within Mini-English in the two later lateral windows
(300--600 ms, `r report_contrast("erp_differential_object_marking_300_600_lateral", "within_Mini-English")`;
400--900 ms, `r report_contrast("erp_differential_object_marking_400_900_lateral", "within_Mini-English")`),
with the Mini-Norwegian contrasts not credible in either.

## Judgement accuracy

Overall judgement accuracy fell across sessions, credibly and substantially, for every
property (gender agreement `r report_effect("accuracy_gender_agreement", "z_recoded_session")`; differential object marking
`r report_effect("accuracy_differential_object_marking", "z_recoded_session")`; verb--object number agreement
`r report_effect("accuracy_verb_object_number_agreement", "z_recoded_session")`). This runs against the direction we had
assumed in setting a positive prior on that term. What fell was the *level* of
performance, while the ability to discriminate held. The grammaticality
effect, which is what indexes knowledge of the property, is credibly positive for
differential object marking
(`r report_effect("accuracy_differential_object_marking", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`)
and verb--object number agreement
(`r report_effect("accuracy_verb_object_number_agreement", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`).
For gender agreement, the average effect is small
(`r report_effect("accuracy_gender_agreement", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`), but it grows
credibly across sessions (see below). Discrimination is therefore present, and improving,
where the level falls. Two features of the design bear on the decline. Properties accumulate
across sessions, so a judgement made at Session 4 is made against a grammar with three
manipulated properties instead of one. The final session, moreover, follows a months-long
interval without exposure, over which some forgetting is expected. We cannot separate these
from a general drift in response criterion, because the design has no condition in which
task demands are held constant while sessions advance. The decline is therefore treated as background against which the discrimination measures
are read, and we draw no conclusion about learning from it.

Against that background, accuracy converged with the ERP development for gender agreement
and diverged for differential object marking. For gender agreement, the learning effect was
credible (grammaticality $\times$ session, `r report_effect("accuracy_gender_agreement", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session")`), as was a
language modulation of it (`r report_effect("accuracy_gender_agreement", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`), advantaging
Mini-Norwegian. The gender effect also strengthened at retention, driven by that group
(within Mini-Norwegian `r report_contrast("accuracy_gender_agreement", "within_Mini-Norwegian")`; Mini-English
`r report_contrast("accuracy_gender_agreement", "within_Mini-English")`). Differential object marking elicited a large grammaticality effect
(`r report_effect("accuracy_differential_object_marking", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`) that nonetheless declined across the retention interval in both
groups (overall `r report_contrast("accuracy_differential_object_marking", "overall")`). Verb--object number agreement showed a strong
grammaticality effect (`r report_effect("accuracy_verb_object_number_agreement", "z_recoded_grammaticality")`) with little net change at retention
(`r report_contrast("accuracy_verb_object_number_agreement", "overall")`).

## Multivariate decoding of grammaticality

We decoded
Grammatical from Ungrammatical trials at each time sample (leave-one-participant-out
AUC; @fig-decoding). Error was controlled across time within each analysis by
cluster-based permutation and, within each property, across the clusters of its pooled
overall time-course by Benjamini--Hochberg FDR (the confirmatory correction family; see
*Transparency, preregistration and analysis status*). A significant
cluster licenses only that the grammaticality time-course as a whole departs from
chance. The temporal boundaries of a surviving cluster are not themselves inferential
claims about the onset, offset or duration of the effect [@sassenhagen2019cluster], and
we do not read them as such.`r decode_status_results()`
<!-- STATUS: the CONFIRMATORY decoding values in this section are final. All three
     properties' pooled overall time-courses now come from the B = 1,000 run and are
     corrected under the per-property confirmatory family. Gender agreement's overall block
     was assembled from its banked checkpoint by scripts/09b_assemble_confirmatory_
     timecourse.R, because the confirmatory family cannot be changed by the exploratory
     blocks that are still running. Those session-resolved breakdowns remain at B = 200 for
     gender agreement only; decode_expl_pending() states that in rendered prose and retires
     itself when they land. -->

```{r}
#| label: fig-decoding
#| fig-cap: "Time-Resolved Multivariate Decoding of Grammaticality per Property"
#| apa-note: "Lines are leave-one-participant-out AUC for the Grammatical against Ungrammatical contrast (overall analysis, all sessions pooled). The dashed line is chance (0.5). The dotted line is the cluster-forming threshold used by the permutation test (the 95th percentile of the pooled within-participant null). Horizontal orange bars mark the temporal extent of clusters in the pooled overall time-course that survive Benjamini--Hochberg FDR correction (q < .05) across that property's overall clusters (each property's family corrected separately), annotated with the cluster-level q, the Benjamini--Hochberg adjusted cluster-level p value. The bars denote cluster membership, not sample-by-sample significance. The session-resolved breakdowns are secondary and carry only their own cluster-level p values (see Transparency, preregistration and analysis status). The AUC line is a point estimate. The pipeline records no per-fold dispersion, so no uncertainty band is available and none is drawn. The pre-stimulus baseline (before critical-word onset at 0 ms) is shaded grey and serves as a negative control: above-chance decoding there indicates a confound and not a violation response. The cluster-level decisions shown are those of the confirmatory family, at the permutation count each artefact records."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5.2
if (decode_ready) {
  ov <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(.decode_props), function(p) {
    d <- decode_tc[[p]]; if (is.null(d)) return(NULL)
    o <- d[d$analysis == "overall", , drop = FALSE]
    if (!nrow(o)) return(NULL)
    o$Property <- .decode_props[[p]]; o
  }))
  ov$Property <- factor(ov$Property, levels = unname(.decode_props))
  # Surviving clusters as intervals (extent + cluster-level q), not per-sample points:
  # a cluster test licenses cluster membership, not sample-by-sample significance.
  clab <- function(q) paste0("q ", sub("^0", "", formatC(q, format = "f", digits = 3)))
  cl <- ov[ov$significant_fdr %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE") & !is.na(ov$cluster_id), , drop = FALSE]
  cl <- if (nrow(cl)) dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(cl, Property, cluster_id),
             x = min(time_ms), xend = max(time_ms), q = dplyr::first(cluster_p_fdr),
             .groups = "drop") else NULL
  # Adjacent clusters can sit close enough that their q labels overprint (gender agreement
  # has two whose centres are 60 ms apart), so stagger the annotation above and below the
  # bar by position within each panel. The y scale is expanded below to make room.
  if (!is.null(cl) && nrow(cl))
    cl <- dplyr::ungroup(dplyr::mutate(
      dplyr::group_by(dplyr::arrange(cl, Property, x), Property),
      .vj = ifelse(dplyr::row_number() %% 2 == 1, -0.6, 1.6)))
  ybar <- min(ov$auc, na.rm = TRUE) - 0.006
  p <- ggplot(ov, aes(time_ms, auc)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = 0, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey92") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_line(aes(y = cluster_threshold), colour = "grey60", linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.45, colour = "grey15") +
    facet_wrap(~ Property, ncol = 1) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.20, 0.05))) +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    labs(x = "Time from critical-word onset (ms)",
         y = "Decoding AUC (Grammatical vs Ungrammatical)") +
    les_theme() +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(2, 8, 12, 8))
  if (!is.null(cl) && nrow(cl)) {
    p <- p +
      geom_segment(data = cl, aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = ybar, yend = ybar),
                   inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1.3) +
      # 2.9 mm is about 8.3 pt, the print floor; the dark ink meets the contrast the
      # vermilion bars fall short of, and position keeps each label tied to its bar.
      geom_text(data = cl, aes(x = (x + xend) / 2, y = ybar, label = clab(q), vjust = .vj),
                inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.9, colour = "grey15")
  }
  print(p)
} else {
  cat("*Decoding time-courses will appear here once scripts 08/09 have run.*")
}
```

The three properties differed here too, though the ordering of their raw separability has
to be read against the pre-stimulus baseline.
Differential object marking, whose univariate signature was the weakest and
shortest-lived, was by far the most separable, though not necessarily by a violation
response: its overall time-course carried
`r dec_count(dec_dom, "n_overall_fdr", "cluster")` surviving FDR correction, peaking post-stimulus at AUC
`r dec_val(dec_dom, "max_auc_ov", 2)` (at `r dec_val(dec_dom, "peak_ms")` ms;
@fig-decoding). The pre-stimulus baseline, which should sit at chance, did so for the
other properties but not for differential object marking, whose pre-stimulus AUC
averaged `r dec_val(dec_dom, "pre_mean_auc", 2)` with
`r dec_count(dec_dom, "pre_n_fdr", "sample")` surviving FDR before the critical word. Its
highest AUC anywhere in the epoch falls in that baseline
(`r dec_val(dec_dom, "pre_max_auc", 2)`), above its post-stimulus peak.
Part of the differential-object-marking separability therefore precedes the stimulus
and may reflect a low-level difference between conditions, for instance the physical
presence of the object marker in the preceding region, and need not reflect a violation
response. Peak AUCs are quoted on the post-stimulus axis for this reason. The extents
of the surviving clusters make the limit concrete: one lies wholly before the critical
word (`r dec_span("differential_object_marking", 1)`) and the other begins just before
onset and spans the epoch (`r dec_span("differential_object_marking", 2)`). The
cluster test cannot attribute any part of the surviving separability specifically to a
violation response. What it establishes is that the conditions are separable throughout
the trial, and the post-stimulus peak set against the pre-stimulus mean bounds how
much separability the violation response could add. A decoder trained at one latency
also classified neighbouring latencies. No null distribution was computed for that
temporal-generalisation pattern, so we describe it without interpreting it.
Gender agreement, whose amplitude effect was credible in the region-averaged models,
produced `r dec_count(dec_gender, "n_overall_fdr", "cluster")` in its pooled time-course
surviving the confirmatory correction (@fig-decoding), spanning
`r paste(dec_fdr_spans("gender_agreement"), collapse = ", ")`. Its smallest cluster-level
`r dec_min_p(dec_gender)` in that pooled time-course`r dec_at_floor(dec_gender)`, reached by
`r dec_n_at_floor("gender_agreement")` of its clusters, and it peaked post-stimulus at AUC
`r dec_val(dec_gender, "max_auc_ov", 2)` (at `r dec_val(dec_gender, "peak_ms")` ms).
Its pre-stimulus baseline sat at chance, so, unlike differential object marking, it carries
no separability that precedes the critical word, and its post-stimulus clusters cannot be
attributed to a difference in the region before it. Verb--object number agreement produced
`r dec_count(dec_verb, "n_overall_fdr", "cluster")` surviving correction in its pooled
time-course (smallest cluster-level `r dec_min_p(dec_verb)` across all its analyses,
before or after correction; peak overall AUC
`r dec_val(dec_verb, "max_auc_ov", 2)`). Cross-language generalisation, in which the
decoder is trained on one mini-language and tested on the other, peaked post-stimulus at
AUC `r dec_val(dec_gender, "max_auc_xlang", 2)` for gender agreement,
`r dec_val(dec_dom, "max_auc_xlang", 2)` for differential object marking and
`r dec_val(dec_verb, "max_auc_xlang", 2)` for verb--object number agreement. Those
values, and the temporal-generalisation ones, are descriptive. No permutation null was
computed for them, so we treat them as converging context and do not read the transfer
question off them.
Cross-property generalisation was near chance in every direction (peak post-stimulus
AUC `r xprop_max()` across all six train--test pairs). This too is descriptive. It has
no permutation null, and because every participant contributes trials to all
three properties, the train and test sets are not participant-independent. Its
theoretical reading is taken up in the Discussion. Because each per-cell decoding
score is a mean cross-validated AUC estimated on cells of differing and sometimes
small participant numbers, the
ordering across properties is provisional, and every cluster-level decision reported here
rests on the well-populated pooled time-course [@varoquaux2018].

# Discussion

We set out to decide whether prior-language influence on early L3
morphosyntax is wholesale or property-by-property. The answer these data return is
selective. Gender agreement, the one property with a first-language analogue, was the
one whose behavioural advantage tracked that analogue, and that advantage grew
credibly across sessions. The two properties novel to both prior languages showed
no such advantage, and their electrophysiological modulations ran in opposite
directions, which neither account predicts. Both families expect any
first-language-congruent advantage to fall on gender agreement, and it did. Their
predictions differ on when it should appear, which the sections below take up.

The three structures were thus acquired on three different trajectories
(the full estimates are in the Results and @fig-erp-forest). Uneven trajectories alone
do not decide between the accounts, since wholesale transfer constrains the initial
state and says nothing about the rate at which individual properties are subsequently
learned. The adjudication below rests on where and when the language effects
appeared. Divergent trajectories within the same learners are in any case an established
pattern. Number
and gender agreement dissociate across the proficiency spectrum in second-language
learners, the feature instantiated in the first language showing a violation response
at lower proficiency than the novel one [@alemanbanon2018]. Brief training can also
produce a developing violation response for
one rule and none for another taught in the same protocol [@davidson2009]. Longitudinal
designs show that a P600 absent at the start of instruction can be present after a
short intensive course, with its magnitude tracking behavioural sensitivity [@white2012].
That supports reading the present session effects as training-driven. Two features of
the design nonetheless limit the reading. Session and training are confounded, so nothing
in the design separates them, and every sentence frame recurs across sessions, so part of
the growth of the grammaticality effect could reflect memory for particular sentences.
The by-item session slopes absorb item-level change in amplitude but do not separate
rule learning from sentence familiarity.

One feature of the grammaticality effect must be stated before its development is
interpreted: its polarity. With grammatical coded $+0.5$, a positive coefficient means
that ungrammatical critical words were the more negative-going. For gender agreement that
holds in every window, including 400--900 ms. That is a sustained violation negativity
where our informative prior anticipated a late positivity. The data overrode that prior,
and the shift under the weak priors was negligible
(see *Priors*). For the two control properties, the effect is positive in the earlier
windows and turns slightly negative by 400--900 ms, though that reversal is not credible
in any cell. A violation negativity in learners at low proficiency has a natural
reading in the developmental ERP literature, where the early stages of morphosyntactic
learning are marked by N400-family negativities that give way to a P600 as proficiency
grows [@osterhout2006]. That literature also finds lexical ERP change within about
fourteen hours of instruction in novices [@mclaughlin2004], a morphosyntactic violation
response within a week of brief training [@davidson2009], and individuals varying along a
negativity-to-positivity continuum in native processing [@tanner2014] and in
learners [@tanner2013]. On that reading, the growth of the
effect across sessions tracks a cohort still on the negativity side of that
trajectory, consistent with the diffuse, non-posterior topography. Averaging across
individuals who differ systematically in component dominance [@tanner2014] would itself
flatten and diffuse the grand-average topography. The non-canonical distribution is
therefore also consistent with a mixture of negativity- and positivity-dominant
responders, and need not imply a single non-canonical generator.

## Relation to the initial-exposure antecedent

Against @gonzalezalonso2020, the closest antecedent, these data replicate the general
profile but not its specifics. Two features carry over. Their learners produced no P600
to gender-agreement violations at first exposure, and neither did ours at any session.
The dominant signature for gender agreement here was a violation negativity in every
window, under a comparable artificial-language paradigm. The measurement occasion was not comparable, since their ERPs
come from a single first-exposure session, whereas ours begin only once a learner has passed
the 80% post-training criterion and continue across four sessions. An early negativity to
gender-agreement violations was likewise present in both studies. The specifics do not
carry over. Their negativity was confined to the English-lexicon group and to right-anterior
electrodes, whereas ours was credible on the midline, diffusely distributed, and not
credibly modulated by language in any window. Their Spanish-lexicon group showed a broad
positivity to violations at 300--600 ms, whereas in our gender-agreement data the
ungrammatical trials were the more negative-going in that window and in the other two.

The divergences admit two kinds of explanation, and the literature on replication cautions
against reaching for the substantive kind first. Substantively, the designs differ in the
first language (Spanish against Norwegian), in the realisation of gender (concord across
the noun phrase against a suffixed determiner with predicate-adjective agreement), and in
the measurement occasion (a single first-exposure session against a trajectory whose first
ERP session follows a training gate). Statistically, their groups comprised 26 and 24
learners. Effects that reach significance in samples of that size systematically
overestimate their true magnitude and can even carry the wrong sign [@gelmancarlin2014].
The significance filter also makes published effects look more replicable than they are
[@vasishth2018], and trial-level measurement error can inflate as well as attenuate an
observed effect, producing spuriously large estimates in small samples [@loken2017]. ERP
effects compound the problem, since even systematic resampling finds the magnitude, onset
and scalp distribution of the P600 to vary widely across samples [@kim2024], so the exact
topography and timing of a violation response are the quantities least likely to
reproduce in any replication, ours included. On that reading, the level at which replication should be assessed is the
qualitative one. There the two studies agree: early-stage learners of a miniature
language respond to morphosyntactic violations with attention-sensitive negativities, and
the canonical P600 is absent until proficiency has grown. The same arguments cut against
over-reading our own group-specific effects, several of which rest on comparably small
cells, and the Strength of evidence section holds them to that standard.

## A signature more property-by-property than wholesale

The two families were set out in the Introduction. The three properties behaved
differently from one another: strong, broadly
distributed learning for gender agreement; for differential object marking an early
grammaticality effect, possibly carrying a stimulus-driven component, that did not
consolidate; and a late, language-conditioned signal for verb--object number agreement.
That heterogeneity sits more naturally with the property-by-property family, though it is
not decisive on its own, for the reason just given. The discriminating observations follow.

Transfer itself is distributed no more evenly than learning is. A credible source-language
modulation appeared for all three properties, but in different measures and with different
signs. For gender agreement, it was behavioural, advantaging the Mini-Norwegian group
(`r report_effect("accuracy_gender_agreement", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`), while its
ERP counterpart stayed near zero. For the other two, it was the reverse, credible in the ERP
signal and not behaviourally, and the two point in opposite directions: positive for
verb--object number agreement
(`r report_effect("erp_verb_object_number_agreement_400_900_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`)
and negative for differential object marking
(`r report_effect("erp_differential_object_marking_400_900_lateral", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language")`).
This is not the pattern we predicted. The design
treats both properties as controls, and neither family predicts a source-language
modulation on them (see *The present study*), yet both showed one, in opposite
directions. The prediction failed, and we have no account of the pair. Another ERP test
of these models with a miniature language met a comparable outcome
[@pereirasoares2022]. The L2 Status Factor derivation in the Introduction would favour
the Mini-English group on every property, which fits the differential-object-marking
modulation and contradicts the other two language effects, so it does not account for
the pair either. A general advantage of one training group is likewise hard to
reconcile with modulations of opposite sign on the two controls. The remaining
candidates, a difference in difficulty or in the amount of exposure each property had
received by Session 6 and a false positive among eighteen cells, are not distinguishable
in these data.

The claim that survives is narrower, and it turns on timing. Under the source selection
the design supports, both families confine any advantage to gender agreement. Where they
differ is its onset: present from the property's first session under wholesale
projection, accruing with exposure under property-by-property transfer. The behavioural
advantage carries both signatures: a credible advantage at the average session
(`r report_effect("accuracy_gender_agreement", "z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_mini_language")`)
and credible growth across sessions (the three-way interaction above). The quantity the
timing question needs is the advantage evaluated at the property's first session, derived
from the same draws: `r first_sess_adv("accuracy_gender_agreement")`. That interval
includes zero, so the onset test is indeterminate on its own terms. It neither establishes
that the advantage was already in place when the property was first probed, which is the
wholesale signature, nor rules it out, and its central tendency leans towards presence.
As set out in the Introduction, growth is what the property-by-property account predicts
and what wholesale projection permits, so the timing evidence favours the former without
settling the contrast. As noted above, heterogeneity on its own is the weaker evidence,
since a sufficiently unconstrained selective account accommodates almost any pattern
[@schwartzsprouse2021].

The language factor sharpens the point. Grammatical gender, expressed in Mini-Norwegian
through a suffixed determiner, recapitulates a structure of the learners' first language
(Norwegian has both grammatical gender and a suffixal definite article). The Mini-English
realisation, an English-like free determiner for a feature English does not encode, has no
such first-language support. Accordingly, the behavioural gender-agreement effect showed a
credible language modulation (the grammaticality $\times$ session $\times$ language
interaction reported in the Results), advantaging the Mini-Norwegian group.
Differential object marking and verb--object number agreement are novel to both Norwegian
and English, and neither showed that first-language-aligned advantage in the behavioural
development. Their ERP modulations therefore cannot be read as first-language congruence
effects. The differential-object-marking one runs the other way: its grammaticality
effect held up across the retention interval for the Mini-English group and not for the
Mini-Norwegian one (@tbl-retention). Both families predict that the one property with a
first-language analogue is the one whose advantage follows it. What neither predicts is
that the two properties without such an analogue should diverge from each other, and a
single grammar projected wholesale offers no more purchase on that divergence than a
property-by-property account does.

The behavioural gender advantage also bears on the L2 Status Factor specifically. On the
derivation set out in the Introduction, an L2 default predicts either no group difference
or an advantage for Mini-English, never one for Mini-Norwegian. The credible Mini-Norwegian advantage on gender agreement therefore runs
directly against an L2 default source in this population, a stronger disconfirmation
than a violated null prediction.

Within the property-by-property family, the data also begin to discriminate. The
Linguistic Proximity Model and the Scalpel Model both allow influence that is
property-specific and, where the match is misleading, non-facilitative, and are
compatible with everything observed. The Cumulative-Enhancement Model's distinctive
claim, that prior languages facilitate or remain neutral, is harder to reconcile with a
modulation whose direction opposes first-language congruence, although on properties
without a source the model makes no clear commitment. We record this as a point on
which the family's members differ, without treating it as a resolved contrast.

## Change across the retention interval

What happened to these effects over the months without exposure depends on how the
retention step is modelled. Under the linear specification, the gender-agreement grammaticality effect was
larger at Session 6 than at Session 4 in both languages and to almost the same degree
(midline 400--900 ms, overall `r report_contrast("erp_gender_agreement_400_900_midline", "overall")`; language difference
`r ret_lang_diff()`). That reading is an extrapolation, since the contrast is the fitted
linear trajectory evaluated over the retention step (see Results) and so reports continued
growth at the training rate. The linear specification cannot express a change specific to the
interval.

The refit that frees the Session-6 offset revises both halves of it.
`r retfree_sentence()` Averaged over languages, the freed offset is credible in
`r retfree_tally("gender_agreement", "overall", "credible")` gender-agreement cells, so the
apparent strengthening was the training trend carried across the gap. What the freed model
does show, in
`r retfree_tally("gender_agreement", "language_difference", "credible")` cells, is a credible
difference between the languages in how the effect changed over the interval (midline
400--900 ms, `r ret_lang_diff(freed = TRUE)`). The Mini-Norwegian estimate is positive in
`r retfree_tally("gender_agreement", "within_Mini-Norwegian", "positive")` cells and the
Mini-English estimate negative in
`r retfree_tally("gender_agreement", "within_Mini-English", "negative")`, although each
group's own change is individually credible in fewer of them (Mini-Norwegian
`r retfree_tally("gender_agreement", "within_Mini-Norwegian", "credible")`, Mini-English
`r retfree_tally("gender_agreement", "within_Mini-English", "credible")`). The average null therefore
reflects two effects cancelling, and the direction of the divergence matters.
The effect was maintained where the learners' first language supplies the same structure and
eroded where it does not. On this evidence, the retention behaviour of gender agreement tracks
the source grammar. We hold the conclusion at the level
the estimates support, which is the group difference and not either group's separate
trajectory, a distinction that comparisons of separately tested effects routinely blur
[@gelmanstern2006; @nieuwenhuis2011]. Verb--object number agreement, by contrast,
gained over the interval only within the Mini-Norwegian group (@tbl-retention). The
latest-introduced property, novel to both prior
languages, strengthened for one training group only. That is a group difference on a
property where property-level congruence predicts none, so we group it with the
unexplained control modulations discussed above, separately from the gender-agreement
transfer effect. The candidate explanations listed there apply here too, and we do not
choose between them. Differential object marking, whose behavioural accuracy declined
across the interval in both groups (@tbl-retention), diverges by language in the freed
model as gender agreement does, but in the opposite direction. Its
retention estimate is negative within Mini-Norwegian in
`r retfree_tally("differential_object_marking", "within_Mini-Norwegian", "negative")` cells, and the
language difference is credible in
`r retfree_tally("differential_object_marking", "language_difference", "credible")` cells (midline
400--900 ms, `r ret_lang_diff("erp_differential_object_marking_400_900_midline", freed = TRUE)`).
That is the same reversal of first-language congruence that its late-window transfer term
shows, which we could not account for there and cannot account for here. This property also
has a stimulus confound the others do not (see Results). We
therefore do not read its retention profile as consolidation of a durable representation.

Consolidation is defined as the continued transformation of an experience-dependent
representation after acquisition, through recurrent reactivation during wake and sleep
and redistribution of the representation to additional sites [@dudai2015], so change
across an interval containing no further training cannot be a practice effect. The
complementary-systems account supplies the mechanism for language specifically: rapid
hippocampally supported familiarisation followed by slow neocortical consolidation, with
cortical responses becoming knowledge-like only where a consolidation opportunity
intervenes [@davis2009]. In the closest precedent, adults trained on an artificial
language showed ERP responses that grew more native-like after months without exposure
while behaviour was unchanged [@morganshort2012plos], and responses to newly learned
words shift measurably across a single overnight interval [@bakker2015]. The
stabilisation-versus-enhancement distinction drawn in the procedural literature
[@robertson2004] frames the profiles here, once the freed estimates replace the
extrapolated ones. Gender agreement shows neither enhancement nor decay on average but a
divergence between the languages, verb--object number agreement gained in Mini-Norwegian
alone, and differential object marking diverged in the opposite direction to gender
agreement. An offline gain of this kind plausibly reflects rule abstraction
[@nieuwenhuis2013; @tamminen2015], though @mirkovic2016 found no sleep benefit
for the systematic aspects of a comparable artificial gender language. That study used a
nap-length interval and behavioural measures, which a longer, electrophysiologically
measured interval may reach past without contradicting.

## Convergence and divergence of the two measures

The electrophysiological and behavioural measures converge for gender agreement in
indexing learning, and, on the derivation that bears on consolidation, at retention as
well. The behavioural gain was carried by the Mini-Norwegian group, and the freed
electrophysiological estimate shows the same language-dependent divergence, with no
credible average change but a credible difference between the languages in the same
direction. It
was the linear extrapolation, which reads the retention step off the training trend, that
made the electrophysiological pattern look language-general.

The two measures diverge more sharply for differential object marking. It elicited a
large, credible behavioural grammaticality effect (Results) even as its ERP
grammaticality effect was credible in a single early cell, and that behavioural
effect then eroded at retention, a dissociation suggesting explicit, strategy-based
judgement of a structure that never became an automatic processing routine. The two
are not redundant, even though they are recorded on the same trials. Where they part
company, they separate the automatic neural response to a violation from the explicit accuracy
of the judgement made about it.

For gender agreement, the dissociation runs the other way. The source-language advantage
was carried by the judgement and not by the electrophysiological response, which suggests
that at this stage first-language congruence shapes the explicit decision more than the
automatic violation response. Where in processing transfer takes effect is a question
the property-by-property models do not yet specify, and this pattern indicates it is
separable from whether transfer occurs. An EEG study of natural-language L3 learners
reports a different division, with first-language similarity consolidating implicit
knowledge and second-language similarity enhancing metalinguistic judgement [@xu2024].
Here the first-language-congruent advantage surfaced in the judgement, so the locus may
vary with the stage of learning as well as with the source.

One behavioural result stands apart from the dissociations. Overall accuracy fell across
sessions for every property, against the improvement under mere exposure that motivated
the prior on the session term [@mueller2009]. The design gives two reasons. Each session
adds a property, so later judgements are made against a larger grammar, and Session 6
follows months without exposure. That the grammaticality effect held or grew while the
level fell indicates that the decline reflects task difficulty or a drift in response
criterion, with the knowledge the effect indexes intact, although the design cannot
separate these.

## What the multivariate analysis adds

With the confirmatory decoding settled, the univariate and multivariate analyses order the
three properties in broadly the same way. Gender agreement carries an amplitude effect
credible in `r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality", "gender_agreement")` cells and
reliable pattern separability. Verb--object number agreement carries neither, though its
grammaticality effect changes across the retention interval. Differential object
marking carries separability that its pre-stimulus
baseline forbids us to read as a violation response. That agreement was not guaranteed,
because the two analyses ask different questions. Window-averaged amplitude asks whether a condition shifts the mean
at a set of electrodes, whereas decoding asks whether the joint sensor pattern separates
single trials [@hebart2018; @wang2024]. A divergence in either direction would not have told
us which property is better represented, and classification accuracy is in any case not a
standardised effect size and cannot be compared across properties as though it were
[@hebart2018]. One limit is worth setting out before the mechanisms. Rejecting a
pooled cluster null licenses only that a grammaticality pattern is decodable in some part
of the sample, leaving its prevalence across participants unestimated [@allefeld2016].

One profile in these data has a documented mechanism, and the profile that would have
raised a puzzle does not arise. A contrast can be decodable with
little univariate effect because decoding tolerates non-uniform response signs, so
neighbouring sensors of opposite polarity both carry information where averaging cancels
them [@hebart2018]. Forward modelling shows that such cancellation is substantial at the
scalp for distributed sources with partly opposing orientations [@ahlfors2010]. The
transient mean amplitude and comparatively high classification of differential object
marking are therefore compatible with a single generator whose spatial configuration is
stable even where its net amplitude is small, so far as the baseline difference allows
that reading. Multivariate analyses of sentence processing have repeatedly
recovered effects that the corresponding ERPs did not [@he2024; @cho2025]. The converse
profile is equally well characterised. Multivariate tests draw their sensitivity from
electrode-level variability in the effect within participants and are insensitive
to the between-participant variance in mean amplitude that governs univariate group
tests [@davis2014, on fMRI voxels], and increased
trial-to-trial variability leaves expected mean amplitude unchanged while progressively
shrinking expected decoding accuracy [@carrasco2024]. An effect that is consistent in
sign but spatially homogeneous would therefore yield a credible amplitude effect
with comparatively little for a classifier to exploit. That profile does not describe
gender agreement here, which separates reliably as well as shifting the mean. Decoding is usually the more sensitive test of
the two, but it is not uniformly so, and comparable orderings are documented for the
mismatch negativity and the N2pc [@carrasco2024].

These considerations constrain the claims available to us. A failure to decode is a failure
to find linearly separable information under one analysis, and it leaves open whether the
brain distinguishes the conditions [@peelen2023]. Classification performance, high or low, is
a poor guide to representational content [@ritchie2019]. Nor would a divergence between the
two analyses, had one arisen, support a conclusion about the dimensionality of the
underlying code [@davis2014].

The null cross-property generalisation bears on a live theoretical question. If the
grammaticality response were largely a domain-general salience or integration signal
[@sassenhagen2019; @aurnhammer2023], a decoder trained on one property should transfer to
the others, but it transferred in no direction. That pattern is consistent with evidence
that the late positivity fractionates topographically and functionally [@kaan2003], that
agreement features follow separable developmental courses [@alemanbanon2018], that
different violation types within the same learners are predicted by different
individual-difference variables [@nichols2019], and that decoders of
grammatical features generalise selectively [@cho2025]. Reliable
cross-context transfer of linear EEG decoders is achievable [@zhao2025], which weighs
against reading the present null as simple insensitivity. Even so, failed
cross-classification is confounded with feature selection, since the sensors and
latencies that best separate grammatical from ungrammatical trials within a property need
not be those carrying a property-general signal [@kaplan2015]. We therefore read the
result as consistent with construction-specific coding, without taking it to refute any
shared component. A Bayes-factor treatment of the decoding time-course would
allow such nulls to be quantified as well as reported [@keysers2020;
@teichmann2022].

## Strength of evidence

The conclusions below should be read on the graded scale set out under *Inference*
[@makowski2019; @kruschke2018]. The gender-agreement learning effect is credible in every
cell but one under both random-effect structures. The between-language difference in how
that effect changed across the retention interval is credible in
`r retfree_tally("gender_agreement", "language_difference", "credible")` cells, with
lower interval bounds close to zero in some of them (@tbl-retention-free), so it is
credible on the stated criterion without being a large effect. The average departure
from the training trend at Session 6 is not. The learning effect in particular is
the most structure-independent result in the paper. The grammaticality $\times$ session
interaction is credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", "gender_agreement")` cells under
the maximal random-effect structure and in the same
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session", "gender_agreement", structure = "base")`
without the by-item slope. The verb--object number development and its
Norwegian-specific retention are better described as suggestive and warrant confirmation,
and the same holds for the differential-object-marking transfer interaction. It is credible in
`r cred_cells("z_recoded_grammaticality:z_recoded_session:z_recoded_mini_language", "differential_object_marking")`
cells, unchanged when the model is refitted under weakly informative priors, and it survived
the move to the maximal structure. It is nonetheless small, and it sits close enough to the
threshold that data-handling decisions taken before any model was fitted could bear on it.
One such decision applies here: four Session-3 datasets were mis-filtered at acquisition
and are excluded from every fit reported, an exclusion justified a priori and applied to
the whole grid. Because no full-sample refit was run, the effect of retaining those datasets
is not estimated.

The decoding evidence grades separately, and unevenly across the three properties. Gender
agreement's `r dec_count(dec_gender, "n_overall_fdr", "cluster")` surviving the
confirmatory correction rest on the full permutation null, on a pre-stimulus baseline at
chance, and are secure on that basis. Differential object marking's
`r dec_count(dec_dom, "n_overall_fdr", "cluster")` are not comparable evidence: both begin
before the critical word and its highest AUC falls in the baseline, so they bound the
separability a violation response could contribute without establishing that it
contributes any. The session-resolved breakdowns enter no correction family and are graded
no higher than descriptive. The
near-absence of a gender-agreement transfer interaction in the ERP signal is a well-estimated
value near zero, though it remains conditional on the prior and the
interval width. The verb--object number and differential-object-marking
signals therefore remain provisional, and the gender-agreement pattern is the secure
result. The property-by-property reading is the account the heterogeneity supports, short
of a decisive refutation of wholesale transfer, which a single study cannot deliver. The transfer
interactions that remain near zero are best understood as
absence of evidence. They do not demonstrate absence. We did not adopt an
equivalence (region-of-practical-equivalence) criterion, so a precisely estimated
coefficient whose direction is undetermined ($p_d \approx .50$) marks a well-localised null
estimate [@amrhein2019; @kruschke2018].

## Limitations and future directions

The strongest constraint on what this design can conclude is how narrowly the two families
of account are separated by it. Only gender agreement has a first-language analogue, so
only gender agreement places the two miniature languages in different relations to a prior
grammar. The other two properties are novel to Norwegian and English alike and serve as
controls. The wholesale-versus-property-by-property
contrast therefore rests on a single dissociating property, which is thin ground for a
claim about the unit of transfer, however the other evidence falls. A design contrasting
two candidate source grammars, or several properties each aligned with a different prior
language, would bear the weight this one is asked to. The heterogeneity we do observe, which runs across properties and measures and includes a
reversal of sign, is more readily
accommodated by a property-by-property account than by a wholesale one, but consistency
with that family is not a decisive test between them. The two
electrophysiological modulations on properties with no first-language analogue are
predicted by neither.

The artificial-language design also buys experimental control at some cost to ecological
validity, and three further features of it constrain the present conclusions. First, the properties
enter at different sessions (gender agreement from Session 2, differential object marking
from Session 3, verb--object number agreement from Session 4), so a property's identity is
confounded with its amount of exposure. Cross-property comparisons of learning and transfer
are therefore not exposure-matched, and the weaker signatures of the later-introduced
properties are in part a difference in training time. An exposure-matched design that introduced the
properties in counterbalanced order would separate the two. Second, the additional
gendered or case-marking languages noted under *Participants* were not screened out.
Such experience could support the gender or marking structures, and it is only partially
absorbed by the L1-dominance covariate, which indexes the standing of the first language
without capturing the breadth of the repertoire, and which moreover enters the ERP models
only. The behavioural models have no such control, so the
behavioural gender advantage is the estimate most exposed to it. Third, effects are
quantified as mean amplitudes in fixed latency windows, with no peak or topographic
decomposition. The absence of a native-speaker ERP baseline also means that the results
speak to the development of the grammaticality response and leave its native-likeness
untested. A
native-speaker baseline would test whether the developing response converges on the native
pattern, and a longer interval whether the divergence between the languages at retention
widens. How far the priors
and the interval widths condition the transfer interactions that remain near zero is
addressed under *Strength of evidence*.

Two features of the sample bear on the retention inference, and a third on every
between-group comparison. Of the `r flow_n("enrolled")` learners enrolled,
`r flow_n("attended_S6")` attended the Session 6 retention test, so the Session 6
estimates draw on the returners alone while the training trend draws on every session,
and the models treat the missing sessions as ignorable given each participant's random
effects. Returners may differ from those who left, and a retention estimate conditioned
on returning need not describe the cohort that began. The 80% training gate described
under *Transparency, preregistration and analysis status* adds a second selection, since
it conditions which participant-sessions contribute data on performance in that session,
and its outcomes are folded into the attendance counts. Assignment to language followed
a fixed rule on the participant identifier, so the groups were not formed by random
allocation, and the between-group comparisons carry the uncertainty that attends a
non-randomised design.

The behavioural judgement task also lacks a stable cross-participant item factor, so item
variance is absorbed into the residual for accuracy (though not for the ERP models, which
use fixed sentence frames). Cognitive individual-difference predictors (working memory,
inhibitory control, statistical-learning ability) are excluded here by design and
analysed in a companion paper [@lesspredictors2026], keeping the present focus on the
linguistic transfer signal.
A natural further step for the decoding strand is
representational similarity analysis [@kriegeskorte2008rsa], which would characterise
what the distributed pattern represents: whether the same neural geometry that separates
grammatical from ungrammatical trials in one property recurs in another. That would be a
stronger test of shared representation than the cross-property generalisation reported
here.

## Conclusion

Tracked from the first post-training session to a post-consolidation retention test,
three morphosyntactic properties followed three different trajectories, and the one
advantage that tracked a first language was confined to the one property that had a
first-language analogue. On these data, transfer is better described as
property-specific than as the projection of a whole grammar. We offer that conclusion
provisionally. Only gender agreement dissociates the two
accounts here, and under the design's own source selection, the wholesale alternative is
disfavoured more by the advantage's growth over sessions than by its location.

# Data and code availability

Data extraction, model fitting and reporting are fully scripted as a reproducible
research compendium [@marwick2018]. Models were fitted on High-Performance Computing
(HPC) clusters at Sigma2 (Norway) and the University of Oxford's Advanced Research
Computing facility, on Linux (`r prov("platform", "*[platform pending a pipeline run]*")`)
under R `r prov("R")` [@rcoreteam], with `brms` `r prov("brms")` [@burkner2017] driving
CmdStan `r prov("CmdStan")` through the `cmdstanr` `r prov("cmdstanr")` backend. The clusters
supply that stack through environment modules, with no container. The compiler settings
used on those clusters are recorded in the repository and do not affect the posterior draws.
Every version given here comes from the provenance record the fitting run wrote. Model
fitting used the fixed seed `r prov("seed:LES_SEED", "20260607")`, set in the shared
Bayesian settings and recorded in that provenance record. The decoding permutations used
the seed `r prov_dec("seed:LES_DECODE_SEED", "20260702")`, exported by the job script that
runs them and recorded by that script beside the decoding artefacts.
This manuscript reads only the script-generated summary tables,
so every statistic in the Results is populated from them and none is transcribed by hand.
The pooled posterior summaries, retention contrasts, convergence diagnostics, sample-flow
counts and decoding time-courses that populate the figures and tables are all published
with the repository. The decoding artefacts include the participant count behind every
per-cell score. Figures are drawn with `ggplot2` [@wickham2016]
using the theme and colour system of `depictr` [@depictr], whose default qualitative
palette is the colourblind-safe Okabe--Ito set. The companion paper [@lesspredictors2026]
uses the same system, so the two share one visual identity. The literature counts in
@fig-literature
were retrieved from the Scopus Search API with `scopusflow` [@scopusflow], which records
the exact query beside each count, so the search is reproducible from the repository. Its
coverage limits are stated in the figure caption. All extraction, modelling and reporting
scripts are archived with the data in the project's Open Science Framework repository at
<https://osf.io/tq7vy>, together with the environment
specification: an `renv` lockfile pinning the R packages of the fitting library, and a
provenance record written at fit time. That record holds the software versions in force
when the ERP models were fitted, which is what the versions above are read from. The
accuracy models and the decoding analyses run in the same cluster environment under
separate scripts. The accuracy script records the R, brms, cmdstanr and CmdStan versions
of each fit in the pooled fit metadata that accompanies the results, and the decoding job
records its seed and permutation settings beside the decoding artefacts. The raw
electroencephalographic recordings, too large to distribute through an ordinary
version-control repository, are held in the same Open Science Framework repository as
the code. The paper's analysis code and other open materials are also available at
<https://github.com/pablobernabeu/LESS-morphosyntactic-transfer>.
